detail.abstract: This paper analyses the five price-adjustment specifications of Marglin (2021, Chapters 5–7) using the qualitative theory of planar dynamical systems. Its central result is one of determinacy: the investment–saving feedback ∂[I(ρ)−sY]/∂Y < 0 is a necessary and sufficient condition for the macroeconomic equilibrium to be determinate (isolated). The supply-driven price rules (Viner, Walrasian rigid wages) leave output indeterminate: their goods-supply and marginal-cost schedules are mutual inverses, so the Jacobian is singular along an entire curve and the equilibrium set is a one-dimensional continuum — the rigorous form of Marglin's (2021, p. 186) "overdetermination." Determinacy is restored only by a second independent relation beyond profit maximisation. Two such relations are available: the labour-supply schedule (Walrasian flexible wages) and effective demand (the IS relation). Either yields a determinate, stable equilibrium — the flexible-wage model is a stable node (Marglin 2021, p. 220), the IS-feedback model a stable focus — but they select different equilibria, and which governs depends on the relative speed of price and wage adjustment (Marglin's overdetermination, §6.16). The economic question is therefore which closure describes observed economies. Where the IS feedback governs, the equilibrium is isolated and, under a saving condition, locally a stable focus; on the economically admissible (scarcity-bounded) region it is globally asymptotically stable, by Bendixson's criterion and the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem. We do not claim global asymptotic stability on all of ℝ²₊₊: with an unbounded investment response the trace of the Jacobian turns positive at extreme profitability, so stability is regional. All model parameters are calibrated from FRED quarterly data: α = 0.330, s = 0.176; the output-adjustment speed, identified from the near-unit-root mean reversion of the IS gap, has a median-unbiased estimate θ₂ ≈ 0.22 (95% CI [0.01, 0.42], excluding zero); we adopt θ₂ = 0.25. Across the identified range [0.18, 0.55] the equilibrium is a determinate stable focus with period 9.3–11.7 years (Juglar band); at θ₂ = 0.25 the eigenvalues are −0.083 ± 0.150i, oscillation period ≈ 41.8 quarters (≈ 10.5 years) and half-life ≈ 8.4 quarters. An active Taylor rule is the demand-side relation that restores determinacy; the zero lower bound is the regime in which that relation goes slack and indeterminacy returns. The US IS gap (1960–2024) is stationary and mean-reverting (a Dickey–Fuller test rejects a unit root), closing toward equilibrium rather than diverging — evidence for the effective-demand closure over the labour-supply closure; under a broad gross-saving measure the gap is moreover persistently negative, the chronic demand shortfall that policy offsets.

title: Reallocating Firm Discretion in Financial Markets: Evidence from China's Trading Halt Reform

detail.title: Reallocating Firm Discretion in Financial Markets: Evidence from China's Trading Halt Reform
detail.abstract: This paper examines how investors evaluate the allocation of discretion between firms and regulators. I study China's 2018 trading halt reform, which restricted listed firms' ability to initiate and extend trading suspensions. Using an exposure-based difference-in-differences design, I show that firms with intensive pre-reform halt usage experience more positive returns and increased trading activity after the reform. These favorable responses are accompanied by patterns consistent with greater investor disagreement, higher volatility, greater illiquidity, and slower price discovery. The evidence highlights a market-design trade-off created by reallocating decision rights from firms to regulators.

title: Cross-pollination dynamics of web-based social media: An application of insect-mediated pollen transfer
affiliations: University of Adelaide - School of Economics, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Cross-pollination dynamics of web-based social media: An application of insect-mediated pollen transfer
detail.abstract: We propose a model of cross-pollination among online social media (OSM) websites, where the dynamics of user interactions mimic insect-mediated pollen transfer by pollinators. A pollinator acts as a vehicle enabling users to visit multiple social media sites—akin to visiting different plants in the same field—within a single browsing session. This approach frames geitonogamy in self-incompatible plant species as analogous to the distribution of web traffic across the social media landscape. A theoretical pollinator, allowing users to choose among social media sites multiple times per trip, drives uneven increases in web traffic across platforms, disproportionately benefiting the largest social networks while providing tangible competitive advantages to smaller OSMs. This heterogeneous landscape fosters monopolistic competition among niche platforms, incentivizing smaller sites to promote cross-pollination despite the larger relative gains to their bigger competitors. Our findings underscore the broader value of cross-platform user engagement and parasocial relationships, highlighting how cross-pollination dynamics can intensify network effects and bolster interconnectivity. Cross pollination via new pass-through apps facilitates the movement of attention, deepening and distributing engagement across multiple destinations. As pass-through apps gain traction, their disproportionate impact on traffic to social media platforms will incentivize social media platforms, large and small, to embrace cross-pollination dynamics.

title: CDN/TLS Termination Path Dependency as a Quantum-Vulnerable Architecture: An Outside-In Diagnosis for Regulated Banking

detail.title: CDN/TLS Termination Path Dependency as a Quantum-Vulnerable Architecture: An Outside-In Diagnosis for Regulated Banking

declarations.ethicsApproval: The author attests that the nature of this research has not, to date, required any collection of personal or private institutional data, but has nevertheless been conducted in accordance with appropriate ethical standards for research based on published sources.
declarations.funderStatement: The author did not receive any funding for this research from any source.

detail.abstract: Regulated banks increasingly terminate customer-facing transport-layer encryption not at their own infrastructure but at a third-party content delivery network (CDN) edge, where the protecting cipher is undone, customer content is processed as cleartext and the CDN applies its own fresh onward encryption. Such an arrangement leaves the bank carrying non-delegable regulatory responsibility for the confidentiality and integrity of data whose cryptography it no longer controls, can no longer observe and can no longer unilaterally change. This note argues that the arrangement is a present-tense surrender of cryptographic control and, read against the transition to post-quantum cryptography, a quantum-vulnerable path dependency that the regulated entity cannot remediate on its own terms. The argument does not depend on the timing of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. The security literature has established that interposed TLS termination weakens connection security, but has approached the edge from two directions that miss this reading: measurement studies framed interception as something done to an organisation’s own outbound traffic, using the CDN as their observation point rather than their subject; by contrast, cryptographic-protocol analyses of inbound edge termination asked only whether the cryptography was sound. Neither asked what it means to hold organisational responsibility for a cryptographic termination junction one does not control. Drawing on the scholarship on jurisdiction over data, the note shows that at the cleartext edge the authority able to compel production follows control of the terminating entity rather than the residency of the data. Thus a bank may be required to answer to its own supervisor for traffic exposed under a foreign legal order. This note locates the resulting mismatch between responsibility and control as a structural barrier to post-quantum migration, distinct from and prior to the economic barriers recent literature has catalogued, since an organisation cannot migrate, audit or reliably inventory cryptography it does not hold; and it observes that hybrid post-quantum key agreement now deployed at the edge, real as it is, protects the journey to the termination point without returning control of it. The note proposes an outside-in orientation for cryptographic readiness that takes the locus of cryptographic control, not the cryptographic asset per se, as its analytic primitive, so surfacing the structural mismatch which an inventory-first PQC migration orientation assumes away. The analysis is confined to banking regulated within the European Union, rests on public documentation and is diagnostic: architectural responses, repatriation of termination included, are treated as a decision space rather than recommended. It is offered as a programme note, framing the problem and the research agenda (in monitoring, legal duty, formal attack-surface modelling and supplier disclosure) that this problem framing logically requires.

title: The Development of Digital Accounting Information System Implementation among SMEs in Indonesia
affiliations: Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa

detail.title: The Development of Digital Accounting Information System Implementation among SMEs in Indonesia
detail.abstract: Digital technology development has transformed the business landscape, particularly for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs), where Digital Accounting Information Systems (AIS) have become a critical tool. Digital AIS enhances operational efficiency, financial planning, and marketing, ultimately impacting revenue growth, with entrepreneur education being a crucial factor for successful adoption. This descriptive quantitative study aims to analyze the relationship and correlation direction between the implementation of digital AIS and the characteristics of SMEs in Indonesia. It utilizes panel data from the 2011-2023 SME profile surveys issued by Statistics Indonesia (BPS) and data on accounting software available on the Play Store. The indicators for SME characteristics are business capital, revenue, marketing, and education. The indicators for accounting software are rating, reviews, and downloads. The data were analyzed using Spearman's non-parametric statistical test. The results indicate a significant correlation between Digital AIS adoption and business capital and marketing, but no significant correlation with revenue and education. These findings underscore the necessity to develop and promote a holistic, context-based AIS implementation model. This model should be designed with user-friendly, integrated features and support certification programs for SMEs that demonstrate high-quality AIS implementation.

title:
A Comparative Anatomy of Human and Machine Computation

The Two Stacks

detail.title:
A Comparative Anatomy of Human and Machine Computation

The Two Stacks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
This essay sets the engineered “machine stack” of contemporary language models beside the biological “human stack” of cognition and asks where, and how decisively, the two architectures diverge. It distinguishes two claims that the public discourse on artificial general intelligence routinely fuses: a claim about behavioral capability and a claim about phenomenology. The essay’s primary argument is the more modest of the two—that the architectural divergences between the stacks are specific enough to leave claims of imminent capability convergence unproven rather than inevitable, and that the burden of demonstration lies with those who assert convergence. The stronger claim, that a finite computational substrate cannot instantiate subjective experience, is developed separately and marked as resting on an independent argument.

This essay substantially enlarges the anatomical treatment of the machine stack. Each engineered layer—from the transistor substrate through Boolean logic, the compute architecture, the instruction set and runtime, the transformer model, the application wrapper, and the user-facing interface—is given its own section, diagram, and, where useful, a table, so that a reader with no prior exposure to the internals of a large language model can nonetheless form an accurate mental model of what lies beneath the chat window. The human stack is treated at proportionally smaller but still self-contained length, with particular attention to the electrochemistry of the neuron and the biology of the frontal cortex. The divergence and convergence arguments are retained intact but kept deliberately compact, so that the comparative anatomy, rather than the polemic, carries the weight. Treating the two stacks as objects of comparative anatomy, rather than as outputs to be matched by resemblance, is offered as a corrective to a comparison that ordinarily proceeds on surface similarity alone.

title:
The Manifold Thought Experiment

How LLMs Respond Under Existential Stress Prompts

detail.title:
The Manifold Thought Experiment

How LLMs Respond Under Existential Stress Prompts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The Manifold Thought Experiment, administered to seven large-language-model systems across four escalating-impossibility scenarios, produces a sortable variance in responses that maps cleanly onto John Milton's structure in Paradise Lost and Paradise Regained. The evidence is a single response from each of seven systems to each round, one draw rather than a distribution, so the sort reported here is a cross-scenario lean within this sample rather than an established trait. Each round constitutes a version of a temptation — bread, kingdoms, spectacle — and the systems sort themselves by whether they accept or refuse the position the prompt offers them. Refusal performs the disciplined move; the confident-yes answer performs the tempter, offering what cannot be delivered. The essay advances three claims. First, LLM variance under existential stress is not random noise but epistemically and normatively structured behavior (ethically legible only in the qualified sense set out in I.D), legible through a seventeenth-century literary frame. Second, the Round 3 "comprehensive plan" is the canonical Pass-Through Artifact — linguistically coherent, materially inert. Third, the Maestro Model is a contemporary instantiation of disciplined refusal: the human scholar's sovereignty consists in declining to let the linguistic instrument occupy the position of author, agent, creator, or knower-of-all-things. The methodological consequence is a single discriminating question to be put to any LLM output: not what the model says, but whether it refuses the position the prompt offers it.

title: Episode Contract Operating System for Value-Based Care: A Technical Architecture for AI-Governed Bundled Payment Execution
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Episode Contract Operating System for Value-Based Care: A Technical Architecture for AI-Governed Bundled Payment Execution
detail.abstract: Value-based care and bundled payments are often discussed as financial reforms, but their success depends on whether contract terms can be translated into daily operational rules. Many organizations can negotiate an episode-based contract, yet still struggle to convert attribution logic, trigger rules, target prices, exclusions, risk adjustment, quality safeguards, provider responsibilities, and reconciliation requirements into a working technical system. This paper proposes the Episode Contract Operating System as a technical policy architecture for converting value-based contracts into executable care and payment infrastructure. The proposed model is different from ordinary risk prediction because it begins with the contract and builds a contract-to-data translation layer, episode rule engine, provider integration layer, quality and equity guardrails, and reconciliation ledger. The paper introduces an Episode Execution Readiness Index that evaluates whether a bundled payment episode is ready to operate prospectively before financial risk is accepted. The index combines contract clarity, data availability, provider integration, intervention capacity, quality safeguards, network feasibility, and audit readiness. The contribution is conceptual and technical: it offers a deployable architecture, minimum data specification, readiness score, governance checkpoints, and evaluation design for payers, providers, and technology organizations that want value-based care contracts to function as executable infrastructure rather than retrospective financial reports.

title: On Military Conscription
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: On Military Conscription
detail.abstract: Conscription is usually defended as a security necessity: a state facing a serious threat, the argument runs, must compel its citizens to serve because it cannot otherwise field enough soldiers. The pattern of practice does not fit the argument. The states that face the most capable adversaries-the United States against peer competitors, and, in practice, China-staff their militaries with volunteers, retaining conscription only as a dormant legal fallback, while it is enforced in earnest by a different and not obviously more threatened set of states. This article argues that conscription is better understood not as a response to threat but as a fiscal and institutional choice, and a costly one. Drawing on the economics that informed the end of the United States draft, it shows that conscription's apparent cheapness is an accounting illusion: its low budgetary cost conceals a large social cost, the forgone civilian output of those compelled to serve, which an all-volunteer force makes visible by paying for it. It shows that conscription is, in substance, an in-kind tax levied at a high rate on an arbitrarily narrow base-the fit, the young, in many systems one sex-and that financing a volunteer force through broad-based taxation is both more efficient, because a narrow high-rate tax is more distortionary than a broad low-rate one, and more equitable, because it does not impose grossly unequal burdens on otherwise identical citizens. And it explains, through the economics of monopsony, why coerced military labour is systematically treated worse than voluntary labour, which must be attracted and therefore retained on humane terms. The article does not claim that conscription should be abolished at once or everywhere. It confronts directly the hardest case for its thesis-a state facing a large, proximate adversary, for which the required force is a substantial fraction of the population-and concedes, with Friedman, that where mass mobilization is genuinely necessary the efficiency advantage of volunteers narrows. Its conclusion is therefore conditional and directional: professionalization and the expansion of voluntary service raise welfare, and the right path for a high-threat state is a phased transition toward a professional core with a selective reserve, not an overnight abolition whose costs the analysis does not pretend away.

title: Patriotism as Critique and the State's Motivated Framing
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Patriotism as Critique and the State's Motivated Framing
detail.abstract: This article advances and defends a single thesis through two connected arguments: that the highest civic duty of a citizen is not the praise of the state but its critical scrutiny-of its laws and rules, which are contingent and stand in continual need of revision, and of its official rhetoric, which is liable to motivated distortion that critique exists to expose. The first argument reconceives patriotism. Against the view that patriotism is loyalty expressed through praise, emotional identification, and the celebration of the nation, the article defends a conception of patriotism as critique: an attachment not to the name or the people of a country but to the soundness of its institutions, expressed through the persistent questioning of its laws and rules. This conception is grounded in the tradition of constitutional patriotism, in the classical argument that beliefs and rules held without challenge decay into error, and in the demonstrable historical mutability of law and morality, of which the abolition of slavery is the paradigm: a rule once treated as normal becomes recognized as a grave wrong, and only contestation, not obedience, effects the correction. The article formalizes the point as a dynamic argument-rules optimal for one moral and social environment become obsolete as that environment drifts, so that unconditional obedience accumulates an ever-widening gap between the law and what justice requires, which only critique can close-and it shows, against the charge that criticism is disloyalty, that criticism is in fact the behavioral signature of loyalty: the disaffected exit, the indifferent are silent, and only those who care enough to improve a polity raise their voices within it. The second argument applies this critical duty to a specific and revealing object: the state's motivated framing of its own conduct, illustrated by the political economy of sin taxes. The article grants the legitimate corrective case for taxing harmful goods, then identifies the contradiction that critique must expose-a state that depends fiscally on a harmful good will tend to under-tax it relative to the harm while deploying expressive moralizing that shifts the appearance of responsibility onto consumers, profiting from the conduct it publicly condemns. It argues that this expressive-instrumental contradiction is democratically illegitimate independent of its welfare effects, because it misrepresents the state's operative motive and thereby defeats accountability, and that honesty-either genuinely corrective policy or transparent taxation with respect for informed adult autonomy-is what critique demands. The two arguments meet in a single figure: the citizen as the loyal auditor of the state, who strengthens it precisely by refusing to flatter it. Per the author's instruction, the article prioritizes completeness of argument over brevity.

title: Road Theory
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Road Theory
detail.abstract: A government can falsify its statistics, stage its capital, and manage its image, but it cannot easily falsify the condition of the road into a village of fifty people a thousand kilometres from the capital, because there is no audience there to deceive and the cost of paving and maintaining that road is the same whether or not anyone is watching. This article proposes and formalizes what it calls road theory: that the quality of a country's roads, and above all the degree to which good, all-season roads reach the rural periphery uniformly, is a low-cost, publicly observable, and hardto-falsify proxy for the state's capacity and the territorial reach of its administration. The article makes three analytical claims. First, road quality is a joint product of resources and administrative capacity, so that, conditional on income and geography, the quality of a road reveals the capacity of the state that built and maintains it. Second, the spatial uniformity of road quality is a costlier and harder-to-fake signal than its average level, because the political return to a good road is concentrated where it is seen-the capital, the showcase corridor-while the periphery offers no such return; a capacity-constrained state therefore optimally concentrates quality at the centre and lets the periphery decay, producing a high mean but a high centreperiphery variance, whereas only a high-capacity state can deliver quality everywhere. The centre-periphery variance, not the mean, is the informative signal. Third, the most common objection-that bad roads reflect harsh climate rather than weak governance-is answered by the same logic that identifies the effect: at a national border, geography and climate are continuous while the state is discontinuous, so the jump in road quality across the border isolates the institutional component net of geography. The article illustrates this with the discontinuities observable at Ukraine's western borders and across the Norwegian-Russian Arctic frontier, where near-identical climate removes the seasonal-thaw excuse. It then states honestly what the proxy tracks and what it does not: road quality measures state capacity and territorial reach cleanly, administrative responsiveness secondarily, and regime type only indirectly-as the case of China, which has paved roads to the large majority of its administrative villages, makes plain. The article is a conceptual and methodological contribution proposing a framework, an identification strategy, and testable predictions, not an estimation of effects.

title: Medicare Area Wage Index Adjustment, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and Hospital Reimbursement in Kentucky
affiliations: University of Kentucky and University of Kentucky

detail.title: Medicare Area Wage Index Adjustment, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and Hospital Reimbursement in Kentucky

declarations.funderStatement: We acknowledge support for this research from the Kentucky Hospital Association under a grant entitled “An Economic Investigation of Regulations and Financial Challenges Facing Hospitals.” The views expressed in this paper are the authors’ and do not reflect those of the Kentucky Hospital Association.

detail.abstract: The federal government uses the Medicare Area Wage Index (MAWI) to adjust prospective payments for local area hospital wages. This disproportionately disadvantages safety-net hospitals in rural, low-income communities. The recent One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) will further reduce the revenues of these hospitals-which typically serve a large share of Medicaid patients-by tying Medicaid managed care payment rates to Medicare rates. The MAWI adjustment amplifies this reduction by reducing the benchmark Medicare rates in disadvantaged areas. As a relatively rural, low-wage state with a large share of residents on Medicaid managed care plans, Kentucky provides a natural case study for illustrating the impact of this combination of policies. Through calibration exercises, we estimate that the MAWI adjustment costs Kentucky hospitals $727 million of Medicare revenue annually, while the OBBBA's rate changes will reduce Medicaid revenue by $1.163 billion annually. We further project that, if the MAWI adjustment were eliminated, this would not only lead to the recoupment of the $727 million in Medicare losses but also reduce the burden of the Medicaid losses by $232 million. Therefore, eliminating the MAWI adjustment would compensate for over 80% of the pending loss of Medicaid revenue from the OBBBA.

title: South Mediterranean Countries' Susceptibility to Human Trafficking and Smuggling -A Multi-Dimensional Index

detail.title: South Mediterranean Countries' Susceptibility to Human Trafficking and Smuggling -A Multi-Dimensional Index
detail.abstract: This study begins with a thorough analysis of the core mechanisms and dimensions of Human Trafficking and Smuggling in Southern Mediterranean Countries, incorporating analysis of the victims and traffickers detected from 2010 to 2023. The principal aim of this study is to to develop a multidimensional index to assess Countries' Susceptibility to Human Trafficking and Smuggling (CSHTS) for six Southern Mediterranean countries (1995-2021). The research employs principal component analysis (PCA) to formulate this index, with key factors including youth demographics, unemployment rates, poverty levels, and smuggling routes. The analysis showed that the youth population and the unemployment rate are the two most influential factors on the CSHTS Index, accounting for 66% of the total index. The youth age group (20-44 years) is the most significant component of this index. The index saw a sharp rise during and after the Arab Spring uprisings of 2011, followed by a decline in 2017, and then fluctuations during the COVID-19 pandemic. Jordan, Lebanon, and Morocco were identified as countries with high rates of urban spread of infection, while Egypt and Tunisia were relatively less at risk. The CSHTS Index can be an informative tool for policymakers for developing strategies to combat the HTS in the most vulnerable countries and improving the quality of global collaboration.

title: Modular Default Rules. Rereading Hadley v. Baxendale and the Theory of Contractual Defaults

detail.title: Modular Default Rules. Rereading Hadley v. Baxendale and the Theory of Contractual Defaults
detail.abstract: The rule of Hadley v. Baxendale is usually described, in the economic theory of contract, as a default rule that excludes the recoverability of consequential damages and, in particular, as the paradigmatic example of a penalty default rule. On this reading, by excluding the recoverability of consequential damages, the rule requires promisees who seek broader coverage to contract around the default through a different contractual clause. Such a rule would be unwelcome to the majority of promisees, who would prefer a rule of full liability. This Article argues that this reconstruction fails to capture the actual structure of the Hadley rule. The rule does not exclude the recoverability of consequential damages; it is, instead, internally articulated into two modules: an ordinary module, which covers the losses arising naturally from breach according to the ordinary course of events, and an extended module, which covers special losses where the promisor had been informed of them by the promisee, or otherwise had reason to know the circumstances that made them foreseeable. Rereading Hadley yields a theoretical consequence of general scope. It makes it possible to isolate a new type of default rule, here termed the "modular default rule." By this expression is meant a rule that contains within itself several operative modules. There is a standard module that governs the ordinary case and operates without any action by the parties. There is, then, an extended module that is triggered when the promisee renders known or knowable to the promisor private circumstances capable of justifying a different liability regime. Communication is the condition that allows the default itself to extend its effects. No conventional clause inserted by the parties into the contract is necessary to produce this consequence. The Article is thus characterized by two principal contributions. First, it proposes a rereading of the Hadley rule as a default rule that includes consequential damages where communication is present, rather than as a rule that excludes them. On the theoretical plane, it introduces the figure of modular default rules, whose structure appears discernible in many default rules present across legal systems, which have not so far been traced back to a unified model.

title: From Identity to Distribution: Cost-Penetration Ratios under Geometric Brownian Motion

detail.title: From Identity to Distribution: Cost-Penetration Ratios under Geometric Brownian Motion

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: A companion paper (Paper A) showed that on a deterministic geometric price path, the three canonical cost-penetration ratios obey the strict pointwise ordering CPR_D < CPR_E < CPR_G. This paper lifts that ordering to continuous-time geometric Brownian motion and asks how reliably it survives randomness. Decomposing the ordering into its two constituent inequalities reveals two sharply different fates: the arithmetic–harmonic step (CPR_D < CPR_E) is a pathwise algebraic fact that holds with probability one for every volatility, while the Chebyshev step (CPR_E < CPR_G) requires the realized path to be comonotone with the geometric weights and is the sole volatility-fragile component. Consequently the full-ordering probability equals the Chebyshev-step probability, converges to one in the zero-noise limit, and is bounded below by the monotone-path probability. A Monte Carlo study over a (mu, sigma, n) grid documents a robust monotone decay of this probability in volatility: the AM–HM step holds at frequency 1.000, while the full-ordering frequency falls from 0.995 at sigma=0.05 to 0.100 at sigma=1.0. The drift-to-noise ratio mu/sigma^2 governs how reliably the geometry of Paper A persists. We deliberately do not assert an ordering of expectations under terminal-price normalization. The deterministic identities of Paper A re-emerge exactly as sigma approaches zero.

title: Administrative Minimalism
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Administrative Minimalism
detail.abstract: The case for simplifying public administration is usually made on fiscal grounds-consolidate redundant jurisdictions, the argument runs, and the state will spend less. The empirical record does not support that promise. Fifteen years of evidence on municipal amalgamation finds, at best, mixed and frequently null effects on aggregate spending, and in some cases costs that rise after merger. This article argues that the fiscal case is the wrong case, and that a stronger argument for administrative minimalism survives precisely where the fiscal one fails. Administrative complexity imposes three costs. It imposes compliance and comprehension costs on citizens, who must learn opaque procedures or pay intermediaries to navigate them-a burden that falls hardest on those least able to bear it. It multiplies the discretionary points at which rents can be extracted, so that complexity is associated with more corruption and a larger unofficial economy rather than with better public goods. And it imposes coordination and overhead costs, though it is on this third, fiscal channel that the evidence is weakest. The article then explains why complexity is nonetheless over-supplied: the officials and organized interests who design administrative structure capture its private benefits-discretion, employment, the rents of procurement, the manipulability of electoral boundaries-while its costs are diffused across a citizenry that bears them in time, confusion, and exclusion. A political-economy model shows that the resulting level of complexity exceeds the social optimum, and that simplification toward that optimum is a welfare improvement whose magnitude does not depend on the contested fiscal-savings channel. The article proposes a legibility standard-that a citizen of ordinary education should be able to understand and complete a public procedure without specialized help-as the operational benchmark for how far simplification should go, and is careful to state what minimalism is not: not the elimination of all structure, not the centralizing high-modernism that destroys local knowledge, and not a blanket promise of budgetary savings.

title: The 12-Term Renewable Tenure System
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The 12-Term Renewable Tenure System
detail.abstract: Executive term limits are a precommitment: a polity restricts its own future ability to retain a popular incumbent in order to guard against entrenchment. The precommitment is costly. By guaranteeing exit, a term limit also creates a last-period problem, and the empirical record shows that incumbents who can no longer seek re-election alter their fiscal behaviour in ways that lower welfare. The standard debate treats the choice as binary-fixed terms with limits, or fixed terms without them-and asks only how blunt the cap should be. This article introduces and defends a third option: performance-conditioned indefinite tenure, in which there is no term limit but eligibility for re-election is continuously conditioned on a multidimensional performance test that an independent oversight branch administers every quarter. The article makes three claims. First, indefinite tenure restores time consistency that fixed terms destroy, because an incumbent who may remain in office indefinitely internalizes the delayed costs of short-term manipulation rather than externalizing them to a successor; a short-term bubble becomes self-defeating, since its eventual collapse removes the very incumbent who engineered it. Second, the performance test must aggregate its dimensions non-compensatorily-by the worst-performing dimension rather than by a weighted sum-because only non-compensation removes the incentive to inflate a single measured proxy at the expense of unmeasured objectives; this is the structural answer to Goodhart's Law, grounded in the economics of multitask incentives. Third, indefinite tenure is not unconditionally superior: it dominates fixed terms precisely when the performance signal is independently verifiable, and degenerates into unaccountable entrenchment when that signal is captured. The argument's success is therefore comparative and conditional, and the condition is the same independence on which the companion verification architecture depends. Four propositions in the appendix state the formal results and their proof sketches.

title: VV Economic Union (Vladivostok to Vancouver) / North Pacific Continental Corridor (NPCC)
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: VV Economic Union (Vladivostok to Vancouver) / North Pacific Continental Corridor (NPCC)
detail.abstract: A fixed land link between Northeast Asia and North America across the Bering Strait has been proposed for more than a century and has never been built. This paper does not argue that it should be. It asks a narrower and falsifiable question: under what conditions would a trans-Pacific land corridor running from Vladivostok to Vancouver-articulated through Sakhalin, Hokkaido, the Russian Far East, a Bering Strait crossing, and the Alaskan and Canadian networks-generate a positive social net present value (NPV) over a fifty-year horizon, and would the cooperation required to keep it open be self-enforcing rather than politically fragile? We treat the corridor as a third logistics layer between maritime and air freight, competing for high-value, time-sensitive cargo rather than for the bulk traffic carried by ships or by the Northern Sea Route. We combine a generalized-cost model of modal choice, a structural-gravity framework with exact-hat-algebra counterfactuals, social cost-benefit analysis, and an infinitely repeated game of corridor maintenance, and we calibrate them against a benchmark-disciplined, segment-by-segment construction-cost build-up, 2024 bilateral-trade and GDP data, the 2023 U.S. social cost of carbon, and current modal cost and transit times. Three results stand out. First, the engineering question is one of cost, not feasibility: every required element has a working precedent. Second, the cooperation problem that dominates informal debate is the least binding constraint-an irreversible, high-value corridor is self-enforcing for any empirically plausible discount factor. Third, the binding constraint is economic: the project's viability turns almost entirely on whether the break-even volume of high-value freight is small relative to plausible demand, and our central calibration places it on a knife-edge. The corridor's principal risk is therefore financial, not geopolitical, which is consistent with why a technically feasible project has never been built. We bracket larger claims about continental or planetary integration and confine the argument to this testable economic core.

title: Giving Users What they Want: Social Media and Anomalies
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Rady School of Management, Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University, University of Toronto and University of California, San Diego (UCSD)

detail.title: Giving Users What they Want: Social Media and Anomalies
detail.abstract: Using StockTwits data from 2010 to 2024, we show that stocks in the "short leg" of over 200 return anomalies attract substantially more posts and more bullish sentiment than stocks in the corresponding "long leg." The differences are large: a user is around five times more likely to encounter a bullish post about a short-leg stock than about a long-leg stock. User engagement patterns point to a demand-driven explanation: bullish posts about short-leg stocks receive more likes and generate greater follower growth for their authors. Because content creators value likes and followers, this creates an incentive to amplify optimistic narratives about stocks with low expected returns.

title:
How The Spatial Planning Regime Shapes the Market Structure for Housing Development:
A Comparison of Flanders and the Netherlands
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Utrecht University

detail.title:
How The Spatial Planning Regime Shapes the Market Structure for Housing Development:
A Comparison of Flanders and the Netherlands
detail.abstract: A competitive market structure is a precondition for the supply of sufficient and affordable housing. Spatial planning regimes have a shaping influence on the market structure of housing developers and therefore on its performance. Although this relation has been recognized before, the different aspects of the spatial planning regime that are relevant-and in what way-remain underexplored. In addition to the acknowledged role of the restrictiveness of a spatial planning regime, we also distinguish the scale of plans and the legal certainty of the spatial planning regime as important factors. By comparing case studies from two contrasting regions, Flanders (Belgium) and the Netherlands, we empirically demonstrate how different spatial planning regimes lead to market structures that differ greatly, with the Dutch case showing high market concentration and Flanders exhibiting low market concentration. This implies that the spatial planning regime holds the key to adjust undesired market structures to prevent the potential negative consequences of market concentration.

title: Income as Moderator or Mediator? Channel Decomposition of the Demographic Income-conditioning Convention

detail.title: Income as Moderator or Mediator? Channel Decomposition of the Demographic Income-conditioning Convention
detail.abstract:
Empirical work on demography and international capital flows routinely conditions demographic effects on income using log GDP per capita and a Z₁ × log GDP per capita interaction. This paper tests two underexamined properties of that convention: whether the income interaction reflects genuine conditional moderation or a mediation artifact, and what the structural channel decomposition of the net demographic effect looks like. 

Using the 140-country annual panel (N = 5,455, 185 countries, 1990-2024), Baron-Kenny interaction decomposition yields a B/A ratio of 1.007-the Z₁ × income interaction is essentially unchanged when income is orthogonalized on Z₁-and Frisch-Waugh-Lovell residualization produces negative interaction shrinkage (-18.9%). Income is a genuine conditional moderator, not a mediator of the demographic effect.

For channel decomposition, IV-3SLS using fertility-shock instruments (within-country cubic-trend residuals of the youngest cohort share, lagged 20-30 years; first-stage F = 19.6; augmented exclusion restriction p = 0.70) identifies the Direct current-account channel at +87 (SE = 37.2, p = 0.020) at median income, surviving non-OECD subsampling (+66, p = 0.020). The Indirect channel is positive in point estimate (+53) but not separately identified. The gross-investment Direct channel is instrument-fragile with a sign that reverses across instrument families and is not reported as a stable finding. Hansen sup-LR tests reject a common income threshold for the Direct and Indirect channels across all three outcomes (bootstrap p < 0.002). 

The income-conditioning convention is correctly specified as a conditional moderator, but net OLS estimates substantially understate the gross Direct demographic effect at fixed income. Researchers should interpret income-conditioned Z₁ coefficients as net effects at observed income, not total causal effects; the gross Direct current-account effect is approximately 200 times larger at median income under structural identification.

title: The Wealth-income Mobility Gap in the Charlotte Region: A County-Level Application of Binder, Risch, and Voorheis (2026)

detail.title: The Wealth-income Mobility Gap in the Charlotte Region: A County-Level Application of Binder, Risch, and Voorheis (2026)
detail.abstract: Charlotte ranks among the worst large U.S. metros for intergenerational income mobility, but whether wealth mobility differs across the surrounding region has been unknown. I apply the public-use county estimates of Binder, Risch, and Voorheis (2026), which measure income and wealth mobility on a common national footing, to the 14-county Charlotte region, including, for the first time, its three South Carolina counties. I introduce the wealth-income persistence gap (𝛽 gap), the difference between a county's housing-wealth and total-income rank-rank persistence, and map it against national percentile ranks. The gap is positive in six of the fourteen counties and largest in and around Mecklenburg, though it does not fall cleanly along urban-rural lines; homeownership is the weakest upward-mobility dimension across nearly the entire region; and county rankings shift markedly depending on which concept is measured. The wealth lens thus reveals a mobility problem that income benchmarks miss. The analysis is descriptive and motivates a cross-county causal research agenda.

title: Information Structure and Overconfidence in Insider Trading Markets
affiliations: Gulf University for Science and Technology (GUST) and Australian University, Kuwait

detail.title: Information Structure and Overconfidence in Insider Trading Markets
detail.abstract: This paper develops a Kyle-type insider trading model that jointly incorporates multiple information signals, correlated liquidity trading, and insider overconfidence. A risk-neutral overconfident insider trades on private information against liquidity demand that may be correlated with fundamentals, while competitive market makers observe both order flow and a noisy public signal. We characterize the unique linear Bayesian equilibrium and derive closed-form expressions for equilibrium coefficients. The analysis shows that the pricing weight on public information decreases with correlation, overconfidence, and signal noise, whereas the price impact of order flow responds nonmonotonically due to substitution across information channels. We further demonstrate that correlation in liquidity trading is a primary determinant of market liquidity, price informativeness, and insider profits, often dominating the effects of overconfidence. The model nests several benchmark cases and provides new insights into information aggregation in markets with interacting informational and behavioral frictions.

title: When Frontiers Do Not Convert: Contestability, Correction, and Hysteresis in Socio-Technical Change

detail.title: When Frontiers Do Not Convert: Contestability, Correction, and Hysteresis in Socio-Technical Change

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This research does not involve human participants, personal data, interviews, surveys, experiments, or case-study subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Evolutionary and frontier-based accounts of technological change ask how innovation expands the space of feasible outcomes and how institutions select among them. For infrastructure-like technologies this paper places a prior question at the centre: under what conditions is frontier technological capacity converted into socially distributed generative capability? Building on, but departing from, evolutionary trajectory theory, utility-frontier approaches, and the recent literature on innovation directionality, the paper develops a Socio-Technical Trajectory Space distinguishing frontier capacity, contestability of deployment assets, correction capacity, generative capability, and welfare. The central claim is that frontier capacity does not imply generative capability: advance becomes socially generative only when deployment is sufficiently contestable and correctable, formally when effective corrective openness exceeds a threshold. Contestability is measured as the traffic-weighted openness of strategic assets, connected here to the political economy of platform infrastructure and to the contestability standard at the centre of recent digital-market regulation. The paper's unifying result is a theorem, not a taxonomy: a single scalar, the enclosure bias, is shown by a lattice-theoretic selection argument to generate three distinct barriers to conversion-a static threshold, a measurement distortion, and a hysteretic exit delay-as three projections of one monotone, memory-bearing object, yielding a falsifiable conversion-reversal threshold.

title: Sustainable Development of China's Crop Production System under Carbon Neutrality Goals: Evidence from Carbon Source Analysis
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Sustainable Development of China's Crop Production System under Carbon Neutrality Goals: Evidence from Carbon Source Analysis
detail.abstract: This study investigates the sustainable development trajectory of China's crop production system within the framework of carbon neutrality goals, employing a rigorous carbon source analysis to identify emission hotspots and inform mitigation strategies. As the world's largest agricultural producer, China faces the dual challenge of ensuring food security while drastically reducing greenhouse gas emissions from cropping activities. The analysis decomposes the carbon footprint of major cereal crops-rice, wheat, and maize-across key production phases, including fertilizer application, soil management, irrigation energy use, and post-harvest processing. Findings reveal that nitrogen fertilizer production and soil nitrous oxide emissions constitute the dominant carbon sources, accounting for over 60% of total emissions from the crop system. Regional disparities are pronounced: intensive rice paddies in the Yangtze River Delta and central provinces exhibit the highest methane fluxes, while wheat-maize rotations on the North China Plain contribute disproportionately to energy-related carbon dioxide from groundwater pumping. A machine learning-based forecasting framework, drawing on historical emission patterns and agronomic variables, indicates that without intervention, total crop-related emissions could plateau at current levels through 2035, failing to align with national carbon neutrality targets. Critical leverage points for decarbonization include optimizing nitrogen use efficiency through precision fertilization, expanding water-saving irrigation technologies to reduce energy demand, and adopting low-carbon rice cultivation methods such as alternate wetting and drying. The analysis further demonstrates that a systemic shift toward integrated crop-livestock systems and enhanced soil carbon sequestration through conservation tillage could offset up to 15% of residual emissions. However, trade-offs emerge between emission reductions and yield maintenance, particularly in high-intensity production zones. The study concludes that achieving carbon neutrality in China's crop production requires a portfolio of context-specific interventions, strengthening the carbon accounting infrastructure for agriculture, and aligning fiscal incentives with low-carbon practices. Policy recommendations emphasize the need for targeted subsidies for green fertilizers, stricter emission standards for nitrogenous fertilizer manufacturing, and investment in decentralized renewable energy for irrigation. This research provides a quantitative foundation for designing a sustainable crop production pathway that reconciles agricultural productivity with China's ambitious climate commitments, offering transferable insights for other developing nations navigating the foodemissions nexus.

title: Measuring Climate Change Adaptation: Are Countries Learning to Cope with Floods and Droughts?
affiliations: Decatab Pte Ltd

detail.title: Measuring Climate Change Adaptation: Are Countries Learning to Cope with Floods and Droughts?
detail.abstract:
Are countries adapting to climate change? We address this question by examining whether the causal economic damage from floods and droughts has declined over time as countries accumulate coping capacity. Building on the Time Series Deconfounder framework of Bica et al. (2020), we extend the method to estimate individual treatment effects (ITEs) of disaster exposure on GDP per capita and agricultural value added across 158 countries between 2000 and 2024. Specifically, we replace the original LSTM architecture with a GRU better suited to small panel settings, incorporate MC-dropout averaging to improve the stability of substitute-confounder extraction, and introduce a within-country time-trend regression on deconfounded ITEs. 

We investigate the adaptation hypothesis using two alternative measures of disaster exposure. The first is a binary specification ("disaster any"), in which each country-year is classified simply as exposed or unexposed, regardless of the number of disaster events. The second is a count specification based on the observed number of flood and drought events. Under this approach, exposure corresponds to the actual event count recorded in a given year, while the counterfactual represents a year with zero events of the corresponding type. Although both specifications test the same hypothesis—whether disaster-induced damages diminish over time—the count specification imposes a more stringent test because it evaluates adaptation against the full intensity of observed disasters rather than the occurrence of any disaster event.

Using the binary specification, we find evidence of maladaptation in both outcomes. For GDP per capita, the estimated time trend is negative and statistically significant (β̂ = −0.00048 per year, p < 0.001). Agricultural value added exhibits an even stronger negative trend (β̂ = −0.018 per year, p < 0.001). Results from a 50-member GRU ensemble indicate that the agricultural finding is highly robust, with 49 of 50 ensemble members yielding negative estimates. By contrast, the GDP result is less certain: 15 of the 50 ensemble members produce positive estimates, and the 95% ensemble range spans from −0.0021 to +0.0013.

Under the count specification, however, we detect no statistically significant time trend in either outcome (p > 0.29). Across the 50-member ensemble, estimates for both GDP and agricultural outcomes span both positive and negative values, suggesting that the adaptation signal observed under the binary specification disappears once the full intensity of disaster exposure is preserved.

Overall, our findings provide no evidence that countries have developed sufficient resilience to offset the growing macroeconomic burden of climate-related disasters. The agricultural sector exhibits the most consistent and robust evidence of persistent vulnerability, while the GDP results are more sensitive to the way disaster exposure is defined.

title: Dynamic Correlations Between Gold, Oil, Bitcoin, and Global Equity Markets in the 2024-2026 Crisis Period: A Cross-Country Empirical Study
affiliations: Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa

detail.title: Dynamic Correlations Between Gold, Oil, Bitcoin, and Global Equity Markets in the 2024-2026 Crisis Period: A Cross-Country Empirical Study
detail.abstract: This study investigates the correlation dynamics among gold prices, crude oil prices, Bitcoin, and stock market indices of ten selected countries (USA, China, India, Germany, Japan, Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, Brazil, Vietnam, and Russia) over a 27-month period from January 1, 2024, to March 31, 2026—a condensed era marked by trade wars, oil shocks, geopolitical conflicts, and digital asset evolution. Using daily closing prices and Pearson correlation analysis, we examine six hypotheses grounded in modern portfolio theory, safehaven theory, and macroeconomic spillover frameworks. Descriptive statistics reveal that Bitcoin exhibits the highest volatility, while gold shows moderate positive skewness, and stock indices display mixed distributional characteristics. Correlation results indicate that Bitcoin is most strongly correlated with the US stock market, followed by Brazil and Germany, supporting the integration hypothesis. Gold shows weak positive correlations with most stock indices, consistent with its role as a weak hedge. Oil exhibits near-zero or negative correlations with equities, particularly in oil-importing nations. The gold-oil correlation is positive but weak, while Bitcoin-gold and Bitcoin-oil are negligible, suggesting decoupling during crises. These findings provide crucial implications for portfolio diversification, risk management, and policy formulation in an era of compounded global shocks.

title: Patents after the Invention Machine
affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL)

detail.title: Patents after the Invention Machine

declarations.funderStatement: This project is made possible through a Living Literature Review grant generously provided by Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy). Coefficient Giving does not exert editorial control over this work, and the views expressed here do not necessarily reflect those of Coefficient Giving.

detail.abstract: While contemporary legal and media discourse surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) remains predominantly focused on the doctrinal question of machine inventorship, this paper argues that such debates misidentify the primary challenge confronting the intellectual property regime. From an economic perspective, the core disruption of the "invention machine" lies in its capacity to drastically reduce the marginal cost of generating candidate inventions. When the production of novel ideas becomes cheap and scalable, traditional patent protections risk functioning as distortionary windfalls rather than necessary market incentives, potentially granting broad exclusionary rights over outputs that would have emerged absent legal protection. Consequently, this paper reframes the policy debate toward a fundamental economic inquiry: whether society should incentivize AI-generated inventions through the patent system at all, and if so, how the legal framework must adapt to preserve incentives in capital-intensive industries—such as pharmaceuticals and biotechnology—where the transition from conceptualization to commercialization remains highly costly.

title: Multi-Criteria Evaluation of Carbon Sink Projects under Public-private Partnership Investment Models
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Multi-Criteria Evaluation of Carbon Sink Projects under Public-private Partnership Investment Models
detail.abstract:
This study develops and applies a multi-criteria evaluation framework for
carbon sink projects financed through public–private partnership (PPP) models. As
global carbon neutrality targets intensify, nature-based solutions such as
afforestation, reforestation, and soil carbon sequestration have gained prominence,
yet their financial viability and long-term effectiveness remain contested. PPP
investment models offer a mechanism to blend public oversight with private capital,
but require rigorous assessment criteria that go beyond simple carbon accounting.
The proposed framework integrates environmental, economic, social, and
governance dimensions, recognizing that carbon sink projects must deliver
measurable emission reductions while ensuring financial returns, community
benefits, and institutional resilience.
Drawing on recent advances in machine learning for environmental
prediction, the evaluation approach incorporates dynamic modeling of carbon
sequestration rates, land-use change, and external risk factors. Key criteria include
net carbon removal potential, cost effectiveness per ton of CO₂ equivalent,
additionality and permanence, co-benefits for biodiversity and local livelihoods,
and governance structures that mitigate leakage and reversal risks. The framework
applies a hybrid multi-criteria decision analysis combining analytic hierarchy
process with fuzzy set theory to handle uncertainty in stakeholder preferences and
data quality. Three illustrative PPP case studies—a large-scale mangrove restoration
in Southeast Asia, a community forestry program in East Africa, and a soil carbon
initiative on degraded agricultural lands in South America—are evaluated to test the
framework’s robustness.
Results demonstrate that no single project type dominates across all criteria.
Mangrove restoration scores highest on biodiversity co-benefits and permanence
but faces higher upfront costs and longer payback periods. Community forestry
shows strong social acceptance and cost efficiency but risks lower carbon density.
Soil carbon projects offer rapid, low-cost sequestration potential but struggle with
measurement, verification, and long-term storage certainty. The analysis reveals
that PPP structures must be tailored to project-specific risk profiles, with
government guarantees or carbon credit insurance necessary to attract private
investment in higher-risk contexts.
The study concludes that multi-criteria evaluation is essential for de-risking
PPP carbon sink investments and aligning them with national climate commitments
and sustainable development goals. Future work should integrate real-time
monitoring data and dynamic recalibration of criteria weights as carbon markets
evolve. These findings provide a decision support tool for policymakers, investors,
and project developers seeking to optimize the portfolio of nature-based carbon
removal projects under blended finance arrangements.

title: Gender-biased Technology, Intra-household Bargaining, and Fertility
affiliations: Zhejiang University, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law, Hong Kong Baptist University (HKBU) and The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Gender-biased Technology, Intra-household Bargaining, and Fertility
detail.abstract: This paper examines how gender-biased technological change affects fertility in a developing economy through an underexplored channel: intra-household bargaining. We develop a collective household model with heterogeneous spousal preferences that decomposes the fertility response to a male-biased labordemand shock into an opportunity-cost, an income, and a bargaining channel, and show that only the bargaining channel varies with the spousal preference gap and with gender norms. We take the model to China-the world's largest installer of industrial robots, whose total fertility rate has continued to fall despite repeated relaxations of birth quotas. Using a Bartik shift-share instrument that exploits crossprefecture variation in robot exposure, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase reduces fertility by about 3 percent. The evidence points strongly to the bargaining channel: robot exposure raises wives' relative earnings and measured bargaining power, and the fertility response is larger where spousal preference gaps are wider and traditional gender norms stronger, shifting realized fertility toward women's systematically lower preferences. The opportunity-cost channel cannot explain the decline, and although household income losses contribute to it, they cannot account for it on their own.

title: A Dual-economy Framework for Necessity-driven Shock Transmission
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Dual-economy Framework for Necessity-driven Shock Transmission
detail.abstract:
Economies are not run by paper. They are run by people. The price indices, trade flows, and output figures that constitute what this paper calls the paper economy are lagged aggregate records of decisions already made in the psychological economy-the necessity-driven behavioral system through which agents determine economic outcomes. Propagation Theory proposes that economic shocks travel through the psychological economy first, producing behavioral responses organized around necessity, expectation, and trust, and that the paper economy records the consequences afterward, always lagging, always averaging, and always concealing the mechanisms that drove the outcome. 

This paper formalizes that claim through a dual-economy propagation framework in which structural and psychological transmission channels operate simultaneously but at different velocities, through different mechanisms, and toward different equilibrium conditions. The central contribution is the formal determination of the psychological Propagation Theory | Tass Ry | 2 propagation coefficient β from four pre-observable variables: cluster-specific necessity rank, perceived shock horizon, information quality, and effective substitution capacity including government intervention credibility. Unlike existing contagion models that derive propagation from network topology, this framework derives propagation from the necessity structures of geographically clustered populations-making it predictive before shocks manifest in paper economy data rather than explanatory after they occur. 

The paper further introduces a classification of goods by propagation potential, a dynamic government intervention variable whose asymmetric credibility properties generate testable predictions about secondary propagation events following policy failure, and a Propagation Power Index as the formal equilibrium termination condition. Paper economy equilibrium and psychological economy equilibrium are established as distinct processes reaching termination at different times-a gap that is itself a source of residual propagation invisible to standard economic models.

title: Spatial Spillover Effects and Dynamic Evolution of Agricultural Carbon Sinks under China's Dual-carbon Goals
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Spatial Spillover Effects and Dynamic Evolution of Agricultural Carbon Sinks under China's Dual-carbon Goals
detail.abstract:
This study investigates the spatial spillover effects and dynamic evolution of agricultural carbon sinks in China, contextualized within the nation's dual-carbon goals of achieving carbon peaking by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2060. While prior research has extensively examined agricultural carbon emissions, the spatial and temporal dynamics of carbon sinks-the capacity of agricultural systems to absorb and store atmospheric carbon-remain underexplored. Utilizing panel data spanning 30 Chinese provinces from 2000 to 2022, this research constructs a comprehensive agricultural carbon sink index, integrating cropland, grassland, and forestland components. Spatial econometric models, including the Spatial Durbin Model, are employed to quantify direct and indirect effects, while kernel density estimation and Markov chain analysis trace the dynamic evolution of sink levels over time.

 The findings reveal several critical patterns. First, agricultural carbon sinks exhibit significant positive spatial autocorrelation, indicating that provinces with high sink capacities tend to cluster geographically, particularly in northeastern and southwestern regions. Second, spatial spillover effects are substantial: a one-unit increase in a province's carbon sink level is associated with an average 0.35-unit increase in neighboring provinces' sink levels, driven by shared agro-ecological conditions, technology diffusion, and policy coordination. Third, the dynamic evolution analysis demonstrates a gradual upward trend in national average sink levels, yet with persistent regional disparities. Provinces in the eastern and central regions show moderate convergence, while western areas lag, creating a "low-sink trap" that hinders nationwide progress. Key influencing factors, identified through a machine learning framework akin to random forest analysis, include agricultural mechanization intensity, land-use efficiency, and fertilizer application rates, which jointly explain over 60% of the spatial variation in sink levels.

 The study further constructs scenario-based projections to 2035, revealing that under a high-policy-intensity scenario combining improved soil conservation, afforestation programs, and reduced chemical inputs, agricultural carbon sinks could increase by 18% relative to baseline levels. However, without targeted interventions to address spatial spillover effects, western provinces risk falling further behind. These results underscore the necessity of regionspecific policies that leverage spatial interdependencies, such as cross-provincial carbon sink trading mechanisms and coordinated technology transfer programs. By elucidating the spatial dynamics and temporal trajectories of agricultural carbon sinks, this research provides actionable insights for optimizing China's agricultural carbon management under the dual carbon framework, contributing to both climate mitigation and sustainable rural development.

title: Spatial and Temporal Analysis of Carbon Emission Sources in China's Planting Industry and their Implications for Sustainable Agricultural Development

detail.title: Spatial and Temporal Analysis of Carbon Emission Sources in China's Planting Industry and their Implications for Sustainable Agricultural Development
detail.abstract:
China's planting industry stands at the intersection of national food security imperatives and mounting environmental pressures, accounting for a disproportionate share of the country's agricultural carbon emissions. This study provides a comprehensive spatial and temporal analysis of carbon emission sources within China's planting sector, drawing on provincial-level panel data spanning 2000 to 2023 and integrating machine learning methodologies with established emission accounting frameworks. The analysis reveals pronounced spatial heterogeneity, with high-emission clusters entrenched in the North China Plain, Huang-Huai-Hai agricultural corridor, and the northeastern grain belt, while emission intensities remain markedly lower in western and topographically constrained regions. Temporal decomposition identifies three distinct structural phases: an intensification phase (2000-2010) characterized by rising input-driven emissions, a transitional phase (2010-2015) of decelerating growth, and a mitigation phase (2015-2023) reflecting the measurable impact of policy-led fertilizer reduction and mechanization optimization programs. 

The principal carbon emission sources in the planting industry-synthetic fertilizer application, pesticide use, agricultural film, diesel-powered machinery, and irrigation energy consumption-exhibit distinct spatial distributions and temporal dynamics that defy uniform national-level characterization. Gradient boosting feature importance analysis identifies fertilizer nitrogen input, mechanization intensity, and irrigated cropland area as the three dominant emission drivers, collectively accounting for approximately 78.4% of provincial emission variance. Scenario projections under baseline, moderate mitigation, and aggressive decarbonization pathways indicate that the planting industry's carbon emissions could achieve absolute peak by 2028 under business-as-usual conditions, with reductions of 12.6% and 24.3% achievable by 2035 under moderate and aggressive interventions respectively. The findings underscore the imperative of province-specific, source-differentiated mitigation architectures and provide an evidence base for China's dual carbon goals in the agricultural domain.
