title: Optimal Deployment of Dynamic Wireless Charging Infrastructure For Battery Electric Buses – A Case Study in Auckland, New Zealand
affiliations: Griffith University, University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland - Faculty of Engineering, University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School and The University of Auckland

detail.title: Optimal Deployment of Dynamic Wireless Charging Infrastructure For Battery Electric Buses – A Case Study in Auckland, New Zealand

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand, 55(4), 1091-1110. DOI:10.1080/03036758.2024.2353737

detail.abstract: Inductive power transfer (IPT) systems offer a promising solution to multiple major hurdles associated with electric vehicles, such as the lack of widespread charging infrastructure, driving range anxiety, and significant charging time. With the aid of IPT systems, dynamic wireless charging enables electric vehicles to be charged when running over the IPT power pads. The objective of this study is to minimise the overall cost of charging infrastructure by optimising the deployment of IPT transmitters and the battery size required to support charging for electric buses. A mixedinteger linear programming model is proposed and solved using the commercial solver Gurobi. Bus route information and the characteristics of electric buses, such as weight, drag coefficient and frontal area, are used as input to run the traffic simulation in SUMO to get time-varying velocity and acceleration data during bus operations. A bus route in Auckland, New Zealand, is used as a case study in the presented numerical experiments. A strong correlation between the velocity of the bus and the state of charge is identified. The largest cost component is the charging pad, followed by the battery.

title: Antitrust in the Age of AI: Is the Consumer Welfare Standard Equipped to Address the Rise of Generative Artificial Intelligence?

detail.title: Antitrust in the Age of AI: Is the Consumer Welfare Standard Equipped to Address the Rise of Generative Artificial Intelligence?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Amidst a period of heightened antitrust scrutiny around today's technology firms, the technology of tomorrow brings new questions and challenges to light. Can generative AI disrupt the technology landscape, heightening competition against incumbent firms? Or will generative AI enable rent-seeking behavior targeted at unsuspecting consumers? And, fundamentally, how does the emergence of generative AI contribute to debates around antitrust policy standards? A review of the relevant academic literature, regulatory publications, and market research reveals that generative AI's interaction with antitrust policy exposes key value tradeoffs, even though generative AI is likely to lower technical barriers to entry in many fields and improve total productivity. Specifically, generative AI's applicability as a tool for personalized marketing, price discrimination, and so-called 'behavioral' discrimination can both (a) lead to increased producer surplus at the expense of consumer surplus and (b) contribute to forms of customer persuasion that may be considered harmful-all depending on one's perspectives on paternalistic policymaking and areas of distinction between consumer surplus and welfare. Furthermore, the likely existence of economies of scale in the market for generative AI highlights the challenge of grappling with incumbent firm power (and potential resulting harm) that can ultimately be tied back to efficiency. Although the long-standing assumption of consumer welfare standard-based antitrust is that market failure is the proverbial lesser of two evils, generative AI may make possible increasingly sophisticated price regulation-a capability that may prove useful to mitigate harm that currently eludes detection under consumer welfare-based antitrust.

title: Agricultural Modernization and Its Effects on Crop Carbon Sink Performance: Evidence from Hubei Province
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Agricultural Modernization and Its Effects on Crop Carbon Sink Performance: Evidence from Hubei Province
detail.abstract: Agricultural modernization in Hubei Province has reshaped the relationship between crop production and carbon sequestration, revealing complex dynamics that challenge simplistic assumptions about agricultural sustainability. This study examines the effects of modernization processes—including mechanization, fertilizer intensification, irrigation improvements, and land consolidation—on the carbon sink performance of major crops across Hubei’s diverse agro-ecological zones from 1997 to 2022. Crop carbon sink performance is assessed through net primary productivity, biomass accumulation, and soil organic carbon retention, integrated into a composite index that accounts for both carbon uptake and emissions from agricultural inputs. Findings indicate that overall crop carbon sinks in Hubei have increased modestly over the study period, but with pronounced spatial heterogeneity and stage-specific characteristics. Early modernization phases, characterized by rapid expansion of machinery and synthetic inputs, initially depressed carbon sink efficiency due to elevated emissions from fertilizers and fuel combustion. As modernization matured, particularly after 2012, improvements in water productivity, precision farming, and residue management enabled partial recovery of sink performance, especially in the Jianghan Plain and eastern hilly regions. However, in the western mountainous areas and northern dryland zones, modernization efforts have yet to translate into enhanced carbon sequestration, constrained by fragmented landholdings and limited adoption of conservation practices. Temporal analysis reveals that the relationship between modernization intensity and sink performance follows an inverted U-shape, where moderate levels of technological adoption optimize carbon benefits, while excessive intensification leads to diminishing returns and net carbon losses. The study further identifies that land transfer policies and scale management have amplified sink performance in consolidated farms, but only when accompanied by green technologies such as controlled irrigation and organic amendments. Conversely, regions experiencing rapid urbanization and farmland loss exhibit declining sink capacity, as conversion of agricultural land to non-agricultural uses disrupts carbon cycles. These findings underscore that agricultural modernization is not inherently beneficial for carbon sinks; its effects are contingent upon the type, intensity, and spatial context of technological interventions. For Hubei Province to align agricultural development with carbon neutrality goals, policy frameworks must prioritize region-specific modernization pathways that integrate carbon-smart practices, protect marginal lands from degradation, and incentivize sustainable intensification. The evidence from this study provides critical insights for designing agricultural modernization strategies that simultaneously boost productivity and enhance the climate mitigation potential of cropping systems.

detail.abstract:
This paper argues that U.S. equity market outcomes emerge from a multi-player, non-cooperative game in which four generational cohorts-Baby Boomers, Generation X, Millennials, and Generation Z-simultaneously execute lifecycle financial planning strategies whose optimal payoffs depend on the strategies of the other cohorts. The model does not predict market returns; it identifies the equilibrium conditions that govern the range and stability of sustainable outcomes. When the equilibrium is stable (all cohorts' strategies are mutually reinforcing), markets can sustain elevated returns and recover quickly from shocks. When the equilibrium becomes unstable (cohort transitions change the payoff structure), the system is vulnerable to regime change. 
The paper constructs a Generational Capital Flow Index (GCFI) using a double-logistic sigmoid lifecycle function, U.S. Census population projections (NP2023), Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF 2022) wealth data, tax policy multipliers calibrated to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, 2025), and a longevity-gender adjustment capturing the $54 trillion horizontal wealth transfer to 28 million widows (Cerulli 2024). Central finding: the current multi-cohort equilibrium has been stable and favorable since approximately 2010 (GCFI rising from 74.2 to 116.6 by 2025). The GCFI plateaus circa 2027-2030 and enters a regime of declining equilibrium stability through the 2030s, as Boomer stage transitions alter the payoff structure for all remaining cohorts. Tax policy modulates the equilibrium's sensitivity but does not prevent the transition. 
The paper presents a falsifiable hypothesis: the multi-cohort equilibrium transition between 2028 and 2032 will produce compressed real S&P 500 returns and extended drawdown recovery periods. Confirmation and disconfirmation criteria are specified. The physical science foundations of this framework-including thermodynamic formalization and neurochemical mechanism-are developed in the companion paper, TQF: Tice Quantum Financial (Tice 2026b).

title: Why Do We Buy What We Buy First? The Role of Early-Life Experiences in Consumer Preference Ordering under Changing Income Levels
affiliations: Government College for Women

detail.title: Why Do We Buy What We Buy First? The Role of Early-Life Experiences in Consumer Preference Ordering under Changing Income Levels
detail.abstract:
This paper focuses on how an individual’s choice of buying something first is influenced by 
their early-life experiences, even when their income changes. According to traditional 
economic theories, decisions are based on price and income, which leads to the assumption 
that if two people earn the same, they will behave in a similar way. However, in reality, it may 
not always be true.
For example, individual A might choose to buy food first, while individual B might priorities 
stationaries, even when their level of incomes is equal. This study tries to understand the 
reason behind this difference in priorities. It suggests that childhood experiences and habits 
play a pivotal role in shaping consumer behaviour. 
The study uses both primary and secondary data. A questionnaire was created on Google 
Forms and shared with around 100 respondents, including students and working individuals
on April 2026 out of which 45 valid responses were received. Reports from various sources 
and secondary data from existing studies in behavioural economics was also used to support 
the analysis. The results show that many people resume following the same spending 
priorities they learned in childhood. This shows that preference for a commodity is not just 
based on income but also on past experiences.
The study adds to the existing research by showing that consumer behaviour is not just based 
on prices and income alone, but also considers past experiences. It helps explain real-life 
differences in spending habits and shows the importance of habits in economic decision-
making.

title: Identification of Carbon Sink Hotspots and Coldspots in Hubei Province's Crop Production System
affiliations: Unaffiliated Author, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Identification of Carbon Sink Hotspots and Coldspots in Hubei Province's Crop Production System
detail.abstract: This study identifies and characterizes carbon sink hotspots and coldspots within the crop production system of Hubei Province, a critical agricultural region in central China. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset of crop yields, sown areas, and cultivation practices from 1997 to 2022, the research employs a net carbon sink accounting framework that integrates photosynthesis-driven carbon sequestration with emissions from agricultural inputs, soil management, and field operations. Spatiotemporal analysis reveals pronounced heterogeneity in carbon sink performance across the province, with distinct stages of evolution. The findings demonstrate that the overall crop production system in Hubei functions as a net carbon sink, yet this capacity exhibits significant spatial clustering. Hotspots, defined as areas with persistently high net carbon sequestration per unit area, are concentrated in the central and eastern plains, particularly the Jianghan Plain and the eastern hilly regions. These areas benefit from high-yielding staple crops such as rice and wheat, coupled with relatively efficient input management. Conversely, coldspots, characterized by low or negative net carbon sequestration, are predominantly located in the mountainous western and southwestern regions, where topographic constraints limit mechanization and intensify emissions from fertilizer use and soil erosion. The dynamic evolution analysis reveals that the spatial pattern of these hotspots and coldspots has remained relatively stable over the 25-year period, though the intensity of carbon sink function has fluctuated in response to changes in crop structure, technological adoption, and policy interventions. The study further identifies a critical transition period around 2005-2010, during which the expansion of high-emission cash crops in certain coldspot areas temporarily reduced the provincial net sink. By mapping these spatial disparities, the research provides a foundational evidence base for targeted climate mitigation strategies. The identification of hotspots suggests priority zones for enhancing carbon sequestration through conservation tillage and optimized crop rotations, while coldspot areas require interventions focused on reducing agricultural emissions, such as precision fertilization and improved residue management. This spatially explicit approach moves beyond aggregate provincial estimates to inform localized agricultural policies that can reconcile food production demands with carbon neutrality goals. The findings underscore the necessity of context-specific management to maximize the climate benefits of crop production systems in Hubei Province

title: Resilience of Crop Carbon Sink Systems to Extreme Weather Events in Hubei Province
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Resilience of Crop Carbon Sink Systems to Extreme Weather Events in Hubei Province
detail.abstract: This study investigates the resilience of crop carbon sink systems in Hubei Province, a key agricultural region in central China, in response to increasing frequency and intensity of extreme weather events. Drawing on a comprehensive analysis of crop production data from 1997 to 2022, the research reveals that Hubei’s crop carbon sink exhibits pronounced stage characteristics, spatial heterogeneity, and dynamic evolution patterns. The total crop carbon sink has generally increased over the study period, driven primarily by expansion of staple grain cultivation and improvements in crop yield per unit area. However, this upward trajectory is punctuated by significant interannual fluctuations, with notable declines occurring during years marked by severe droughts, floods, and heatwaves. Spatial analysis demonstrates that the central and eastern plains of Hubei, which account for the majority of the province’s agricultural output, display the highest carbon sink densities but also the greatest vulnerability to climatic anomalies. In contrast, the western mountainous regions contribute less to overall carbon sequestration but exhibit comparatively higher stability due to diversified cropping systems and lower exposure to compound extreme events. The dynamic evolution analysis indicates a gradual shift in the spatial center of gravity of crop carbon sinks toward the northern and eastern parts of the province, a trend that may amplify systemic risk as these areas face increasing drought stress under projected climate scenarios. The findings underscore that the resilience of Hubei’s crop carbon sink system is not uniform but is mediated by crop type, regional climatic conditions, and agricultural management practices. Rice paddies, which dominate the regional carbon sink, are particularly sensitive to water stress and temperature extremes, whereas dryland crops such as maize and rapeseed demonstrate moderate adaptive capacity. The study highlights the necessity of incorporating climate resilience into agricultural carbon management strategies, including diversification of crop varieties, optimization of planting schedules, and adoption of water-saving irrigation technologies. Furthermore, the spatial disparities identified call for region-specific adaptation policies that enhance the robustness of carbon sink functions in high-yield zones while preserving the stability of marginal areas. These insights are critical for designing effective climate mitigation and food security strategies in Hubei Province and analogous agricultural regions facing escalating climate risks .

title: Britain's Struggle with Infrastructure Appraisal: From Optimisation to Navigation
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: Britain's Struggle with Infrastructure Appraisal: From Optimisation to Navigation
detail.abstract: This paper examines Britain's contemporary struggle with infrastructure appraisal through the Department for Transport's Better Connected: A Strategy for Integrated Transport. The report calls for a 'new lens', places people at the centre of appraisal, and commits government to optimising decision-making. These statements reveal a deeper tension within British infrastructure thought. The country's appraisal tradition emerged from a long history of abstraction, measurement and representation, through which complex realities were rendered legible to the state. Cost-benefit analysis became the institutional expression of that tradition. Yet complexity science challenges the assumptions on which optimisation rests. Infrastructure systems are not fixed landscapes containing stable objectives and known alternatives. They are evolving fields in which technologies, institutions, behaviours and possibilities emerge through time. The paper argues that infrastructure should be understood not merely as object or service, but as an intervention that transforms the state of society, market and government. The task of appraisal is therefore not simply to optimise among represented futures, but to navigate futures that are still becoming. Britain's struggle with CBA is thus part of a wider epistemic transition from optimisation to navigation.

title: On the Modeling of Imitation in North-South Endogenous Growth Theory
affiliations: University of Edinburgh, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and University of Macau - Department of Economics

detail.title: On the Modeling of Imitation in North-South Endogenous Growth Theory
detail.abstract: This paper examines three distinct approaches to modeling technological imitation within a North-South endogenous growth framework. We formally compare the analytical properties and quantitative implications of these three alternatives. We show that each formulation yields the same set of core qualitative predictions and we derive explicit parameter conditions under which the formulations are equivalent. However, their quantitative predictions regarding the impact of strengthening intellectual property rights can differ sharply. We conclude with recommendations for researchers in the area.

title: The European Union and Its Alternatives
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The European Union and Its Alternatives
detail.abstract: Why does labour move so little across the borders of the European Union, and what does this immobility imply for the design of European integration? This article argues that linguistic heterogeneity imposes a measurable transaction cost on cross-border mobility, and that this cost helps to explain why the euro area functions poorly as an optimum currency area. We develop a transaction-cost model in which the gains from integration in any given policy domain must be weighed against a communication cost that rises with the linguistic distance between members, and we show that the welfare-maximising architecture under heterogeneous linguistic distance is differentiated rather than uniform. We test the central mechanism with a gravity model of bilateral migrant stocks among thirty-one European states, estimated by Poisson pseudomaximum-likelihood with origin and destination fixed effects. Sharing a common official language more than doubles the bilateral migrant stock once geography, economic size and multilateral resistance are held constant, and a graded effect of linguistic proximity survives in a broader European sample. These results provide fresh micro-level evidence for a long-standing macro intuition in optimum-currency-area theory, and they reframe the European Union's existing pattern of differentiated integration not as a failure of political will but as an efficient adaptation to linguistic heterogeneity. The argument has direct implications for the institutional design of integration among consolidated democracies.

title: Carbon Pricing in EU, Evaluation of the Relationship Between Carbon Emissions and Reflections on Türkiye
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Carbon Pricing in EU, Evaluation of the Relationship Between Carbon Emissions and Reflections on Türkiye
detail.abstract:
This study examines the role of carbon pricing mechanisms in decarbonization efforts, focusing specifically on emissions trading systems (ETS) and the Border Carbon Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). It begins by providing an overview of the historical development of the European Union’s climate policies, then addresses the fundamentals of carbon pricing. The impacts of carbon taxes on economic structures and environmental objectives are assessed. The study examines the development of the cap-and-trade system within the European Union in detail, assessing the effectiveness of the ETS in supporting decarbonization goals. It also evaluates scenarios for Türkiye that include the ETS in the context of the effects of carbon emission reduction policies on real growth. 

In addition, the study attempts to analyze the CBAM, which regulates production and trade environments with the aim of promoting sustainable practices, in terms of its impacts on international trade and competitiveness. The study contextualizes the findings by examining the impacts of the ETS and CBAM on Türkiye, assessing Türkiye’s current climate policies and strategies to integrate the ETS into a broader framework for climate mitigation. 

In this context, the focus is on calculation and monitoring strategies for CBAM compliance with impacts on key sectors such as iron, steel, aluminum, fertilizer, electricity and cement. The study attempts to estimate the cost impacts of CBAM implementation in Türkiye on emissions and local industries, and attempts to evaluate potential commercial losses or gains from CBAM through calculations. Through these insights, the study offers policy recommendations to align Türkiye’s carbon reduction strategies with global decarbonization standards, aiming to balance environmental sustainability with economic stability.

title: Axiomatic Foundations of Negation-based Economics: From Parsing Operators to Asset Pricing

detail.title: Axiomatic Foundations of Negation-based Economics: From Parsing Operators to Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: Negation-based Economics proposes a core proposition distinct from mainstream asset pricing theory: the value of an asset does not reside in its own attributes, but in its relations of exclusion against alternatives. This paper establishes the axiomatic foundation of this proposition. Five core axioms form a complete generative chain from "parsing" to "value." We introduce the parsing operator, the negation channel, and channel closure as core mathematical objects, and formulate the Asset Generation Condition, the Negation-based Representation of Value, and the Negation-based Representation of Pricing. The axiomatic path is independent of traditional economics' reliance on historical transaction data and probability distributions, providing a unified mathematical foundation for treating emerging economic objects not yet assetizedlow-altitude airspace, data assets, carbon emission allowances.

title: Urban Reconstruction and Political Dynamics in Ukraine
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Urban Reconstruction and Political Dynamics in Ukraine
detail.abstract: Postwar reconstruction concentrates unprecedented external resources in territories whose institutions are weak and whose economic geography is uneven. We ask which political forces govern where reconstruction translates into measurable recovery. Combining two strands of the development literature, we treat recovery as jointly determined by internal political institutions (anti-corruption enforcement and governance quality) and external political-geographic integration (proximity to the European Union border and the spatial allocation of EU reconstruction finance). We construct a monthly panel of subnational economic recovery for Ukraine from 2021 to 2026, proxied by VIIRS night-time lights, and link it to verified data on the EU Ukraine Facility, the European Investment Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, to national and subnational corruption and governance indicators, and to controls for war intensity. The empirical strategy adjudicates the classic institutions-versus-geography debate at the subnational scale, using two-way fixed effects, a spatial Durbin model for cross-region spillovers, staggered difference-indifferences robust to treatment-effect heterogeneity, and causal mediation through investment. The central hypothesis is one of complementarity: the marginal effect of EU reconstruction finance on recovery is conditional on local governance quality, so that aid yields more light where corruption is lower. Documented stylised facts-an east-west recovery gradient and a measurable governance shortfall-are consistent with this mechanism. The study offers a template for measuring the political economy of reconstruction in real time and informs the spatial targeting of recovery finance.

title: Horseshoe Diffusions: Heavy-Tailed Generators for Multimodal Generative Models
affiliations: , University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Horseshoe Diffusions: Heavy-Tailed Generators for Multimodal Generative Models
detail.abstract: We introduce horseshoe diffusions, a class of Markov processes whose stationary law has the horseshoe distribution of Carvalho, Polson and Scott (2010) as its marginal-a global-local Gaussian scale mixture with a logarithmic singularity at the origin and Cauchy-type tails. We construct the process as a reversible overdamped Langevin diffusion on an augmented state space carrying a latent log-scale coordinate, identify its generator, and prove that its stationary marginal is exactly the horseshoe law. We then develop the analytic theory of the terminal law. We obtain a closed form for the horseshoe density in terms of the exponential integral, from which we derive a sharp small-ball estimate P(|X| ≤ ε) ≍ ε log(1/ε)-a logarithmic excess of mass at the origin relative to a Gaussian reference-together with regularly varying tail asymptotics, the non-existence of a first moment, and an impossibility theorem ruling out sub-exponential concentration. We complement these with a conditional concentration inequality that isolates the heavy-tailed contribution. Our main probabilistic result is an exit-time separation: for a multi-well target potential, the mean inter-well transition time is exponential in the barrier height for a Brownian-driven Langevin sampler, but only polynomial for the horseshoe diffusion. The proof rests on a single-big-scale-excursion principle that plays the role of the Freidlin-Wentzell large-deviation analysis in the heavy-tailed regime. Finally we give a time-reversal formula for the generative reverse process. The results provide a rigorous probabilistic account of why heavy-tailed, origin-spiked generators traverse multimodal landscapes far more efficiently than Gaussian diffusions.

title: The Impact of ESG Performance on Financial Profitability: Evidence from Tunisia (2021-2025)

detail.title: The Impact of ESG Performance on Financial Profitability: Evidence from Tunisia (2021-2025)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: the author declares no cometing interest

detail.abstract:
This study examines the relationship between Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance and financial profitability among Tunisian firms listed on the Bourse des Valeurs Mobilières de Tunis (BVMT) over the period 2021-2025. Using a panel dataset comprising 100 firm-year observations across 20 leading companies spanning Banking, Agribusiness, Insurance, Industry, and Retail sectors, we employ pooled ordinary least squares (OLS) regression to evaluate whether superior ESG practices translate into enhanced accounting profitability. 
Our composite ESG score, constructed from nine sub-criteria weighted 40% Environmental, 30% Social, and 30% Governance, reveals a statistically significant positive association between ESG performance and both Return on Assets (ROA) and Return on Equity (ROE). Specifically, a one-point improvement in the ESG score is associated with a 1.50 percentage point increase in ROA and a 1.64 percentage point increase in ROE. 
When controlling firm size and financial leverage, the ESG coefficient remains positive and significant for ROA, while the effect on ROE becomes marginally significant. These findings provide robust empirical support for the stakeholder theory proposition that sustainable business practices constitute a value-creating strategic lever rather than a mere regulatory cost, even within the institutional context of an emerging North African frontier market.

detail.abstract: India's e-commerce and platform economy has grown at an extraordinary pace, generating millions of daily digital transactions across consumer marketplaces, freelancer platforms, software-as-a service providers, and financial technology applications. The surge in digital commerce has been accompanied by an equally dramatic rise in payment-related disputes, cases involving non delivery, service deficiencies, fraud, partial performance, and refund failures. Yet the Indian legal system currently lacks a clear, integrated framework to address a deceptively simple but practically urgent question: when a buyer and a seller disagree about a transaction that has already been paid for, who holds the money, on what legal basis, and for how long? This paper examines the case for escrow-based online arbitration as a legally coherent mechanism for resolving digital platform disputes in India. Drawing upon the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the Mediation Act, 2023, and the Reserve Bank of India's Payment Aggregators Directions, 2025, the paper argues that escrow can function as a form of digital interim relief, securing disputed funds during online arbitral proceedings until a neutral decision-maker determines the appropriate disbursement. The paper analyses the legal validity of electronic arbitration agreements in platform contracts, the structural role of payment aggregators under the 2025 RBI framework, the implications of the Supreme Court's ruling in Emaar MGF Land Ltd. v. Aftab Singh for consumer disputes, and the policy developments emerging from NITI Aayog's ODR Policy Plan. It concludes with a six-part proposed framework for integrating escrow, online arbitration, and payment regulation into a workable dispute resolution model for India's digital economy.

title: Social Prescribing and Arts Prescribing in the US: An Implementation Science Study of Models, Barriers, and Facilitators

detail.title: Social Prescribing and Arts Prescribing in the US: An Implementation Science Study of Models, Barriers, and Facilitators
detail.abstract: As Social Prescribing (SP) and Arts Prescribing (AP) expand globally, context-specific research on program delivery and effectiveness is needed. To date, no implementation science research has been conducted in the United States (US), where the healthcare system differs from other countries with large-scale SP programs. This implementation science study used quantitative and qualitative methods to examine perspectives of managers, staff, and service users in nine SP programs in the US and identify barriers and facilitators to SP program delivery and engagement. Quantitative data from surveys were analyzed descriptively. Qualitative data from surveys and interviews were analyzed using framework analysis. The study found high levels of program acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility. We identified 29 themes related to facilitators and barriers. Strong relationships and program alignment with goals and interests emerged as key facilitators. Lack of collective understanding of SP and lack of systems for sustainable funding emerged as key barriers. This study builds on global knowledge and expands understanding of SP in the US context, particularly programs prescribing arts and cultural activities. The themes developed from this study may guide SP program delivery in the US and other countries with private or private/public health systems.

title: An Adversarial Nine-Gate Validation Framework for Distributional Claims Under Fat Tails

detail.title: An Adversarial Nine-Gate Validation Framework for Distributional Claims Under Fat Tails
detail.abstract: Standard validation methodology for quantitative financial signals rests on a foundation of Gaussian assumptions: Sharpe ratio testing, t-tests on mean returns, and Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions all measure performance in a metric space defined by finite moments and mean-driven dynamics. We argue that this foundation is systematically ill-suited for signals that operate through distributional tail mechanisms rather than mean effects, and that the resulting methodological mismatch produces both false negatives (robust signals dismissed by inappropriate metrics) and false positives (spurious signals certified by metrics that cannot detect their pathology).

title: The Digital Spending Trap: How Internet Platform Architecture Systematically Dismantles Household Financial Self-Regulation Across Asia, Europe and the United States

detail.title: The Digital Spending Trap: How Internet Platform Architecture Systematically Dismantles Household Financial Self-Regulation Across Asia, Europe and the United States
detail.abstract: In April 2020, the United States personal savings rate reached a monthly peak of 33.7% in April 2020, the highest recorded figure since the Bureau of Economic Analysis began tracking the measure in 1959. By December 2025 it had fallen to 3.6%, less than half its long-term historical average of 8.4%. In the same period, the global Buy Now Pay Later market grew from a marginal fintech product to a $560.1 billion gross merchandise value ecosystem serving 380 million users across sixteen major economies. Global social commerce expanded from approximately $1 trillion to $2.6 trillion. TikTok Shop alone generated $15.82 billion in US sales in 2025, growing 108% in a single year. This paper argues that these movements are not independent. The collapse of household savings across Asia, Europe and the United States and the simultaneous explosion of BNPL adoption and social commerce are causally connected through three internet platform mechanisms that together constitute a unified system of household financial welfare extraction: the Frictionless Debt Architecture of BNPL credit design, the Algorithmic Commerce Engine of social commerce platforms, and the Cognitive Friction Elimination of dark pattern checkout design. Drawing on secondary data from the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Bank for International Settlements, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Financial Conduct Authority and regional fintech market databases spanning 2020 to 2025 across sixteen markets in Asia, Europe and the United States, this paper introduces the Digital Spending Trap Framework and the Frictionless Debt Architecture as original theoretical constructs, presents five empirical findings establishing the cross-regional operation of the trap at population scale, and identifies the policy and regulatory interventions required to restore household financial self-regulation in the internet platform economy.

title: Housing Affordability: A Decadal Analysis of Private Rents and Youth Earnings in Hong Kong

detail.title: Housing Affordability: A Decadal Analysis of Private Rents and Youth Earnings in Hong Kong
detail.abstract: This study investigates the relative growth trajectories of average private housing rent and median monthly earnings for young workers aged 25 to 34 in Hong Kong from 2014 to 2024. Using data from the Rating and Valuation department, and the Consensus and Statistics department, empirical findings suggest a distinct divergence within the period. Between 2014 to 2018, both real rent and real median earnings experienced upwards growth (+11.2% and +15.2%), driven by supply constraints and an inelastic housing market. For Post-2018, real rent declined while the wage rate for young workers increased, attributed to the macroeconomic shocks such as domestic social conflicts and Covid 19 pandemic. Consequently, this provides a statistical answer that the average median monthly earnings for early workers have outpaced the increase in average private rental costs. However, despite the statistical trend of an increase in "affordability", the absolute financial burden of housing remains oppressive. While current research examines broader economic trends between private rent and earnings, this paper provides a highly localized and age-stratified assessment of affordability of housing in Hong Kong.

title: Financial Carpet Bombing: Swift Sanctions, Moral Authority, and the Multipolar Financial Order

detail.title: Financial Carpet Bombing: Swift Sanctions, Moral Authority, and the Multipolar Financial Order
detail.abstract: SWIFT sanctions function as financial carpet bombing: fast, indiscriminate, and ultimately self-defeating. This paper argues that wholesale exclusion of states from the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) trading short-term coercive pain for long-term erosion of moral authority, while simultaneously accelerating the very multipolar financial architecture such sanctions are designed to deter. Drawing on the literature of economic statecraft, game theory, and international monetary order, the analysis identifies four structural failures of the SWIFT-exclusion model: an informationasymmetry problem that inverts the prisoner's dilemma, a deterrence paradox in which the threat of exclusion is more valuable than its exercise, a regime-propaganda windfall that converts civilian pain into anti-Western recruitment, and a third-party bleed dynamic that exports de-dollarisation to the Global South. The paper further critiques the softpower alternative-encrypted communications, stablecoin rails, civil-society funding-as insufficiently attentive to the counter-information capabilities of contemporary authoritarian states. It concludes that the West faces a binary choice: administer SWIFT as global financial stewardship infrastructure or wield it as a sovereign coercive weapon. It cannot sustain both roles indefinitely.

detail.abstract: The study examines psychological distress, awareness of mental health services and government initiatives, and attitudes towards help-seeking among young Indians in the period after the main waves of COVID-19. It seeks to identify where the gap between need and care lies and what policymakers can do to narrow it. Methodology: The study employed a cross-sectional research design. The researchers used a selfadministered online questionnaire and distributed it via snowball sampling to collect data from 122 respondents. The collected data is then analysed using IBM SPSS. The internal consistency of the eight-item attitude scale was evaluated using Cronbach's alpha. Preliminary data were summarised using descriptive statistics, while Pearson correlation and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) were used to examine the variables. Findings: The study found that psychological distress is common among the young Indian respondents (39.3%). Overall, attitudes towards mental health care are strongly positive: 90.2% of respondents felt services should be more accessible, and 86.9% viewed seeking help as normal. However, only 16.4% had ever actually sought professional help, and 32.0% still feared judgement, revealing a clear gap between attitude and behaviour. These positive attitudes are held regardless of a respondent's level of distress. Awareness of government initiatives was low, at 46.7% for Tele-MANAS and 23.0% for the National Mental Health Programme, and remote service options were among the least preferred. Originality: Recent Indian studies tend to examine either literacy, attitudes or distress, i.e., one question at a time. Using recent primary data on young Indians, this study addresses all these questions, including awareness, in a way the reviewed literature rarely offers.

title: Housing, Financial Capability, and Retirement Security: Structural Constraints and Opportunities in the Visegrad Countries

detail.title: Housing, Financial Capability, and Retirement Security: Structural Constraints and Opportunities in the Visegrad Countries
detail.abstract: This study examines key determinants of retirement security in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) with focus on the endogenous linkages among residential housing assets, households' financial capability, fiscal frameworks, credit market maturity, and long-term care infrastructure. In comparative institutional analysis of the Visegrad Four (V4) countries (i.e., the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia), we evaluate the structural and behavioral frictions that may drive late-life economic vulnerabilities. While the regional pervasive high homeownership rates might be considered historically defensive, in the absence of high level of financial education in competitive developed financial market, it likely contributes to the challenges elderly cohorts face in late-life consumption smoothing, contributing to rising poverty rates and deteriorating living conditions. We highlight the escalating socioeconomic stress, compounded by declining savings capacity, housing equity lock-in, financial exclusion, and institutional misalignment. Beyond reflections and comparisons, the paper aims to provide a learning experience from best-practice retirement development to facilitate active aging and efficient intergenerational transfer not only of wealth but also of know-how, traditions, and dying-out arts and skills. Overall, we contribute to the pension economics literature by positioning housing as a central yet inadequately governed component of retirement systems in aging post-transition economies. The findings carry direct implications for coordinated policy reform across housing, finance, and social protection.

title: Contextualized Benchmarking: A Systems-Informed Framework for Cross-Context Learning and Localization

detail.title: Contextualized Benchmarking: A Systems-Informed Framework for Cross-Context Learning and Localization
detail.abstract: A Systems-Informed Framework for Cross-Context Learning and Localization Benchmarking is often treated as an objective comparison of performance. In reality, organizations operate under profoundly unequal conditions. Regulatory systems, infrastructure quality, market maturity, donor environments, geography, climate, and institutional capacity all shape what performance becomes possible. Yet many benchmarking exercises continue to compare outcomes without adequately distinguishing structural advantage from organizational capability. The result is a persistent risk: context-driven differences are interpreted as management superiority, while locally legitimate models are undervalued because they do not resemble systems built elsewhere. This paper proposes contextualized benchmarking as a systems-informed framework for explanatory comparison rather than simple rank ordering. The framework separates performance into three interacting layers: context, sector logic, and organizational capability. Its purpose is not to weaken comparison, but to make comparison more strategically useful, particularly in cross-regional learning and localization contexts where transferability matters more than imitation. The framework is designed primarily for heterogeneous systems where organizations share a mission but operate under materially different structural conditions, including humanitarian operations, food systems, public health, and social protection ecosystems. This paper argues that benchmarking becomes more decision-useful when it moves beyond ranking and becomes a method for explained comparison. Contextualized benchmarking enables organizations to distinguish between structural constraint and organizational capability while preserving the ability to learn across regions and systems. The central contribution of the framework is the introduction of explicit transferability judgment into benchmarking interpretation. Rather than assuming that visible success should be replicated, the framework distinguishes between practices that are directly transferable, adaptable with redesign, or fundamentally context-bound. Localization is not the rejection of external learning. It is the discipline of converting external learning into locally legitimate design.

title: Ecosystem Strategy and Financial Performance: A Comparative Analysis of Apple, Samsung, and Alphabet
affiliations: Penn State University

detail.title: Ecosystem Strategy and Financial Performance: A Comparative Analysis of Apple, Samsung, and Alphabet
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether Apple’s closed ecosystem strategy is associated with stronger financial and supply chain performance than Samsung’s open ecosystem and Alphabet’s hybrid ecosystem. Using gross margin and inventory turnover data from 2014 to 2024, the study compares the three companies to evaluate how different ecosystem models relate to profitability and operational efficiency. The analysis finds that Apple’s gross margin increased steadily over the period, particularly after 2020, while Samsung’s margins were more volatile and Alphabet maintained the highest margins due to its software and advertising-focused business model. In terms of supply chain performance, Apple consistently achieved substantially higher inventory turnover than Samsung, indicating greater operational efficiency and demand forecasting capability. The findings suggest that a highly integrated ecosystem may provide advantages through stronger customer retention, pricing power, and supply chain coordination. However, differences in business models and revenue structures limit direct comparability across firms. Overall, the study highlights the relationship between ecosystem strategy and long-term business performance in the technology industry.

title: Exploring Hindrances to Undergraduates Opting for Media Studies Career in Sukkur Pakistan
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Exploring Hindrances to Undergraduates Opting for Media Studies Career in Sukkur Pakistan
detail.abstract:
This report explores the hurdles that stops undergraduate students in Sukkur, Pakistan from pursuing studies in media programs . Beside the continuously increasing value of media in building and transforming societal values and public view points, there is to much visible misrepresentation of students in media studies careers. Using qualitative research process involving semi-structured interviews with ten undergraduate media studies students, this analysis identifies main hurdles including parental expectations, societal and cultural pressures, and cultural biases.

The results shows that many students deal with marked pressure from their parents to select more conventional esteemed and financially stable professions such as engineering, doctoral , or business studies. Cultural perspectives and prejudices regarding the instability and lack of respect associated with media careers further increase these challenges. This paper shows the need for decided interventions and policy changes to promote a much better diverse and collaborative environment for students inquisitive in media profession. By solving these hurdles, it is possible to support more students to choose their passions and dreams for media, thereby improving the career with multiple perspectives and skills.

title: An Analytical Review of Tech Mahindra's Margin Expansion through a Human Capital Lens
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: An Analytical Review of Tech Mahindra's Margin Expansion through a Human Capital Lens
detail.abstract:
Tech Mahindra is executing a margin recovery strategy under Project Fortius that is structurally dangerous. While the recent doubling of the EBIT margin to 11.27% is mathematically accurate, the mechanism driving it—talent pyramid dilution and the systematic hollowing out of middle management—has generated a massive, undocumented forward liability.

This investigation, built upon five quantitative models, reveals a base-case FY26 structural exposure of ₹1,645.30 Cr, escalating to a stress-tested exposure of ₹1,751.87 Cr. 

The core failure is an unsustainable junior-to-middle management Span of Control (SoC), currently sitting at an industry-worst 9.29:1. This bottleneck leaves over 16,000 headcount effectively unsupervised, triggering a hidden effective enterprise churn rate of 50.6%. Critically, this structural fragility guarantees a catastrophic reliance on expensive external subcontractors the moment Vision 2027 revenue growth targets are achieved.

To neutralize this threat, the Board must authorize Option B: a targeted ₹143.89 Cr capital injection to repair the SoC via internal promotions. This intervention prevents the imminent margin snap-back and halts the internal human capital bleed. Tech Mahindra is currently operating on borrowed time; they have become lighter, not stronger.

title: Cultural Personalities as Catalysts for Social Harmony: The Role of Zubeen Garg in Contemporary Assam
affiliations: H.P.B. Girls' College, Golaghat

detail.title: Cultural Personalities as Catalysts for Social Harmony: The Role of Zubeen Garg in Contemporary Assam
detail.abstract: Differences in political ideology, religion, language, and ethnicity have historically posed challenges to social cohesion in Assam. Despite these divisive forces, the region's cultural personalities have played a pivotal role in sustaining social harmony since the era of Srimanta Sankaradeva (15 th-16 th Century). While the British colonial policy of divide and rule adversely affected intercommunity relations, cultural personalities such as Jyoti Prasad Agarwala and Bishnu Prasad Rabha preserved the legacy of social harmony initiated by Sankaradeva. They were succeeded by Dr. Bhupen Hazarika, who continued this mission through his artistic expressions. Since the last decade of the 20 th century, Zubeen Garg emerged as a significant cultural figure contributing to social harmony in Assam. This paper examines how Zubeen Garg endeavoured to neutralize divisive social forces in contemporary times. Drawing on observational analysis and secondary sources, the study argues that despite challenges such as neoliberal expansion, the rise of national populism, separatist movements, and tensions surrounding ethnic and linguistic identities, Zubeen Garg successfully sustained social harmony in Assam through his simplicity, humanism, embodiment of multiple identities, and integration of emotional appeal with rational discourse.

title: Gain-Loss Asymmetry and Bimodal Structures in Multiscale Financial Returns: Disentangling Market Dynamics from Random Walks
affiliations: and Universidad Veracruzana

detail.title: Gain-Loss Asymmetry and Bimodal Structures in Multiscale Financial Returns: Disentangling Market Dynamics from Random Walks
detail.abstract: This study presents a multi-scale statistical analysis of financial market dynamics by examining "Trend Returns" (TReturns)-logarithmic returns derived from uninterrupted directional price movements-across four major global indices (DJIA, Nasdaq, Nikkei, and IPC). By contrasting empirical data against a Monte Carlo Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM) null model, we rigorously distinguish between mechanical artifacts and genuine structural anomalies. We analyze Bimodality in TReturns: while daily returns (d = 1) exhibit unimodal noise, trends persisting for d ≥ 2 structurally separate into distinct positive and negative modes. While the GBM confirms that this separation is largely a natural topology of trend persistence, empirical data reveal a distinct divergence at longer durations (d > 6), where the negative mode extinguishes, transitioning back to a positively shifted unimodality-a behavior absent in the persistent bimodality of the random walk. Furthermore, we uncovered a fundamental Dual Asymmetry. While the Asymmetry of Frequency (preference for long uptrends) is partially consistent with positive drift, the Asymmetry of Character-quantified via Volatility Ratios (< 1) and the Wasserstein Distance-reveals that downtrends are structurally more volatile ("violent") and possess heavier tails than uptrends, a feature that the Gaussian control fundamentally fails to reproduce. At the macro level, this manifests as a universal negative skewness. These findings suggest that standard Gaussian models are structurally blind to the specific mechanics of market corrections, leading to systematic underestimation of tail risk.

title: Ecosystem Competition: Platforms, Subsidiary Markets and Multihoming in the Videogames Industry

detail.abstract: Emerging licensing regimes that generate revenue from game sales, along with gamers' consideration of video game purchases in their platform adoption decisions, call for a reexamination of traditional models of platform competition. We develop a novel model of competition between ecosystems, defined by platforms and their console-specific subsidiary markets for video games, to incorporate post-adoption factors into platform pricing decisions. Counterintuitively, our results show that access to additional surplus from game sales intensifies competition, forcing platforms to further subsidize the gamer side. In the absence of royalties, publishers' licensing fees remain unaffected even when the subsidiary market is considered; however, these fees increase under royalty transfers, suggesting that monetary considerations dominate in ecosystem competition. When publishers multihome, the role of the subsidiary market becomes more pronounced: gamerside subsidies deepen while platforms impose higher licensing fees. The subsidiary market also induces greater multihoming than predicted by traditional licensing models. Surprisingly, the effect of royalties on platforms becomes non-monotonic, in contrast to scenarios where all publishers singlehome. This leads to a threshold beyond which platforms may no longer prefer multihoming, diverging from conventional models where multihoming is typically advantageous. Overall, our findings highlight that platforms' strategic responses to gamers' post-adoption behavior and royalty-based licensing structures cannot be inferred through simple extensions of existing frameworks.

title:

Evidence from Saudi Arabia's Post-vision 2030 Reforms

detail.title:
Okun's Law in a Rentier Labor Market: 
Evidence from Saudi Arabia's Post-vision 2030 Reforms
detail.abstract: While the OECD Okun coefficient typically ranges from-0.3 to-0.5, we find a long-run multiplier for Saudi Arabia of only-0.066, roughly one-seventh the international norm. Using revised GASTAT chain-linked seasonally adjusted GDP volumes and 20 quarters of Labor Force Survey microdata (2021Q1-2025Q4), we test Okun's Law in a resource-dependent, administratively managed labor market "one-way ratchet" labor market: administrative policy creates an employment floor that GDP contractions cannot break, but growth alone cannot substantially raise.

title: Remembering Wholeness: Toward a Living Theory of Transformation & Wholeness-based Leadership

detail.title: Remembering Wholeness: Toward a Living Theory of Transformation & Wholeness-based Leadership
detail.abstract:
This white paper establishes the ontological, pedagogical, and developmental foundations of Wholeness-Based Leadership — a One Humanity Leadership approach. Emerging from doctoral research and expanded through scholarship and field-based practice, it articulates a worldview, a living theory of transformation, and a learning architecture for a wholeness-oriented approach to leadership and human development.

It responds to a defining condition of our time: a world shaped by the myth of separation — visible in institutional fragmentation, ecological degradation, burnout, polarization, and epistemological division. These are not isolated crises but expressions of a deeper rupture in how we understand reality and our place within it.

Grounded in an ontology of oneness, this work reframes learning as remembering, leadership as attunement, and development as iterative repatterning across chronological time (Chronos) and transformational thresholds (Kairos). Drawing from quantum science, systems thinking, neuroscience, developmental theory, philosophy, contemplative traditions, and Indigenous wisdom, it holds scientific and spiritual ways of knowing in disciplined dialogue.

The paper advances three aims: to articulate connectedness as the ground of leadership and learning; to present a theory describing movement from separation toward coherence; and to establish a pedagogical architecture integrating whole-person, whole-being, and whole-system development within a participatory field framework.

Its central claim is direct: contemporary leadership challenges cannot be resolved through structural reform alone. They require the cultivation of inner technologies — capacities of perception, attention, coherence, and ethical stewardship — through which leaders learn to sense and shape the fields they inhabit.

This is also a dissertation of the heart. Not a conventional treatise but a weaving of lived experience, scholarship, and intuitive knowing. Across quantum physics, ecology, mysticism, and Indigenous science, a shared insight emerges: beneath fragmentation lies coherence. We are not separate entities but expressions of a living field of Being. Wholeness is not perfection; it is interdependence — the felt experience of belonging within diversity.

The human being is the primary instrument of leadership and systems change. To lead well is not merely to acquire frameworks but to refine the instrument itself — cultivating discernment, alignment, and precision in perception. In a world saturated with noise, the task is not to perceive more, but to perceive more accurately.

A more expanded version of this paper is available upon request.

detail.abstract: Sobolieva, Labov, and Nielsen's article on Russia's war on Ukraine offers a valuable interdisciplinary account of how the conflict has reshaped Europe, with particular consequences for Central and Eastern Europe (CEE). This paper accepts their core insight that the war has moved CEE closer to the strategic centre of European politics, but argues that the analysis must be extended through a sharper account of Europe's internal strategic split.1 The paper develops the concept of an intra-European strategic divergence between Eastern fear and Western indirectness. Eastern European states, shaped by Soviet domination, geographical exposure, and collective memory of imperial coercion, often interpret Russia as an existential threat and therefore support faster, harder responses. Western European states, while broadly supportive of Ukraine, tend to operate through indirect containment: sanctions, arms transfers, intelligence coordination, diplomatic pressure, economic pressure, and calibrated ambiguity designed to avoid direct NATO-Russia confrontation. The argument is not that Eastern Europe is irrational or that Western Europe is cowardly. Both camps are rational within different historical memories and strategic constraints. Eastern Europe reasons from trauma and proximity; Western Europe reasons from escalation control, energy vulnerability, nuclear caution, and dependence on the United States. Using the author's Third Generation of International Relations framework, the paper argues that Ukraine has become a structural frontier, a symbolic battlefield, and a mirror of Europe's unresolved dependency. The war has revealed not only Russian aggression, but also the limits of second-generation diplomacy, where declarations, sanctions, and moral solidarity often exceed institutional capacity, defence production, and credible guarantees.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Demographic Load Doctrine: the principle that population growth from any source becomes a national-resilience issue when it exceeds the adaptive capacity of the systems required to sustain it. Using U.S. Census Bureau population projections through 2100, USDA farmland data, USDA Economic Research Service water-scarcity and productivity analysis, Bureau of Labor Statistics consumer-price frameworks, and national-resilience concepts, the paper evaluates population growth as a capacity question rather than as an immigration-policy conclusion.

The doctrine is intentionally non-prescriptive. It does not recommend an immigration statute, admissions ceiling, enforcement posture, population target, or partisan outcome. Instead, it uses official Census scenarios as neutral demographic anchors and asks how alternative population trajectories interact with agricultural land availability, water-constrained productive capacity, agricultural productivity, infrastructure load, consumer-price pressure, household affordability, and institutional resilience. Immigration is treated only as one variable within official population projections, not as the paper’s moral, political, or statutory subject.

The central finding is restrained but significant: the United States remains capable, yet its strategic margin may tighten if demographic load rises while agricultural land and water-secure productive capacity decline. USDA data show approximately 880.1 million acres of land in farms in 2022, alongside a 20.1 million-acre decline from 2017 to 2022 and a 6.2 percent decline from 2002 to 2022. Census scenarios produce materially different 2100 population outcomes, ranging from approximately 226 million residents under the zero-immigration scenario to approximately 435 million under the high-immigration scenario. When compared against the 2022 farmland baseline, those scenarios generate materially different agricultural acres-per-person ratios.

The paper does not treat these ratios as famine measures. They are strategic-margin indicators. Agricultural productivity has historically offset land, labor, and input constraints; USDA productivity data show that U.S. farm output nearly tripled from 1948 to 2021 while aggregate input use declined slightly. Productivity is therefore treated as the principal counterweight to demographic load. Yet productivity is not assumed to be unlimited. Future gains depend on water reliability, energy stability, fertilizer access, infrastructure performance, labor capacity, capital investment, human judgment, and institutional coordination.

The doctrine further argues that capacity stress becomes nationally significant when it transmits into household and institutional systems. Food, housing, water, and energy are low-elasticity necessities. When price pressure in these categories exceeds household absorption capacity, burden may transfer upward into state and federal support systems through increased demand for food assistance, housing support, utility relief, healthcare subsidies, emergency management, school meals, local services, and stabilization programs. The paper identifies this pathway as household-to-institutional load transfer.

The Demographic Load Doctrine therefore reframes population policy as capacity policy. Its contribution is not a new dataset, but an integrated analytical framework connecting demographic projections, agricultural land trends, water constraints, productivity evidence, consumer-price transmission, household burden, institutional load, and national resilience. It concludes that policymakers should assess capacity before crisis: a republic should measure whether its food, water, land, housing, energy, infrastructure, and household-affordability systems can sustain projected demographic load before scarcity becomes visible as household stress or institutional strain.

detail.abstract: Problem. AI assistants increasingly mediate how prospective customers locate small and local businesses, yet the major AI crawlers (OpenAI GPTBot, Anthropic ClaudeBot, Perplexity) fetch web pages without executing JavaScript, so any content injected client-side is absent from what they retrieve on a direct crawl. Method. We captured each website twice on a single pass: once rendered in a headless Chromium browser with full JavaScript execution (approximating Googlebot's renderer) and once as raw HTML from one HTTP GET sent with a GPTBot user agent and no JavaScript execution, then diffed the answer-critical elements between the two captures. Sample. The sample is a purposive set of 405 North American small-business and B2B websites spanning four verticals; 368 (90.9%) returned analyzable dual captures and constitute the analysis set. Result. 25.0% of analyzable sites (95% CI 20.8-29.7) had at least one answer-critical element present in the rendered DOM but absent from the raw fetch, and 14.7% (95% CI 11.4-18.7) had contact information (phone, email, or postal address) that was invisible to the non-rendering fetch. Interpretation. The largest descriptive difference was by platform: sites on managed builders that server-render by default (Wix and Webflow, grouped) were AI-invisible 4.0% of the time versus 28.3% for all other platforms (two-proportion z = 3.69, p < .001), inverting the common assumption that hosted builders are worse for discoverability than custom builds. Contribution and scope. Findings are descriptive, scoped to direct-crawl visibility on site homepages of a non-representative sample; we release the full per-site dataset under CC BY 4.0 for independent reanalysis. Definition. Throughout, we define answer-critical elements as the content a search or AI system would use to identify, describe, contact, or navigate a business: body text, headings (H1), internal navigation links, contact details (phone, email, postal address), contact or booking forms, and structured data (JSON-LD).

detail.abstract: The paper was to study the factors and impacts of migration in a drought-affected village in district Shahdol, Madhya Pradesh based on primary data using qualitative research methods. The main livelihood strategies of the selected village revolved around agriculture, forestry, and migration. Farmers grew rice during the kharif season and mostly left their fields fallow during the winter. Sal, mahua, tendu, and chaar dominated the surrounding woodlands which also supplied firewood. Villagers engaged in the collection of mahua flowers and tendu leaves during the spring. Growing population in the village created pressure on the traditional livelihoods. Degradation of common property resources were also reflected in the dwindling population and degrading health of livestock. Many local people were demanding pattas in the forest lands due to uneven land distribution and its fragmentation over generations. Monsoon droughts occasionally dried up standing crops and impacted non-timber forest products (NTFPs) collections. Governments took several initiatives for drought management and livelihoods generation. On the other hand, contractors began visiting the village to recruit labourers for sugarcane harvesting in western Uttar Pradesh. With more and more villagers joining the migration streams, migration became one of the mainstream livelihood strategies. Every year during the agricultural lean season, the socioeconomically marginalised people in the village migrated out for employment. A drought year might witness more people joining the streams and for longer durations. Many people traced their first migration during a drought year when their local livelihoods got damaged. Migration allowed people to survive as well as accumulate capital and skill and also challenged wage divide. The implications of migration as an adaptation strategy in the drought-affected village was contingent upon certain contextual factors as the study highlighted.

title: The AI Commons Framework: Private Ordering as Systemic Co-Regulation Across AI Value Chains

detail.title: The AI Commons Framework: Private Ordering as Systemic Co-Regulation Across AI Value Chains
detail.abstract: The most public questions of the AI transition are answered in its most private documents. The AI Act and analogous regimes govern whether a system is safe and rights-respecting enough to be placed on the market and kept there, scaled to risk. They are not built to reach a second class of question the same transition raises, no less a matter of public interest: the distributional, environmental, and participatory stakes of a deployment – who captures the value it generates, who bears its costs, what its compute consumes and emits, who has standing when its terms change. Those stakes take shape at the layer regulation is least able to reach: the operational terms under which capabilities are contracted into use. API conditions, procurement clauses, platform agreements, cloud and compute contracts: each decides something narrower than the public-interest question – a price, a hosting region, a data right, a notice period – and the narrow decisions, together with everything the documents leave unsaid, accumulate into a systemic distributional shape no contracting party has deliberately chosen. This is the interaction-layer governance gap: systemic consequences emerge from operational decisions, and the contracts governing those decisions have no vocabulary for the public-interest commitments the consequences call for. The AI Commons (AIC) Framework is the private ordering mechanism this paper proposes for the space. The framework draws on the Creative Commons and open-source precedent – small families of standardised terms that reshaped how knowledge and code circulate, without statutory change – and applies the same mechanism downstream from the artefact to the deployment. Its six licence profiles – Governance, Sustainability, Openness, Reciprocity, Value, Access – are organised around a paired diagnostic of externality and exclusion, can be activated in any combination and scoped along the value chain, and travel through ordinary contract law. Whether such a regime achieves network effects depends on institutional choices made above it, including how the AI Act’s own infrastructure interfaces with private ordering above the regulatory floor. Read against the Act, AIC is also a mode of implementation: the Act’s own toolkit already reaches for voluntary model contract terms and codes of conduct, and AIC generalises that instrument class to the questions the Act cannot pose. AIC is systemic co-regulation: a co-equal mechanism, lateral through value chains where public regulation is vertical through jurisdictions, operating as a formal innovation in how governance commitments propagate.

title: Voice and State Capacity: The Rise of Indigenous Lobbying in Ottawa
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management

detail.title: Voice and State Capacity: The Rise of Indigenous Lobbying in Ottawa
detail.abstract: In October 2015, Justin Trudeau was elected Prime Minister of Canada on a platform that placed reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples at its center. This report documents that, in the ten years since that election, Indigenous lobbying in Canada's federal registry increased by over 2,000 percent, while all other lobbying grew by roughly 300 percent. In the same period, the number of unique Indigenous organizations registered to lobby federally nearly quintupled. The substantive focus of Indigenous lobbying also shifted: the generic tag Aboriginal Affairs fell from 41 percent to 27 percent of lobbying tags, while Economic Development rose from 18 percent to 29 percent. These patterns reflect a substantial expansion in Indigenous federal political engagement; whether that expansion has translated into corresponding policy outcomes-and whether capacity to engage federally is evenly distributed across communities-are separate questions that this report flags but does not resolve. 1 Throughout this report, the term "Indigenous" is used as an umbrella term referring collectively to First Nations, Métis, and Inuit peoples. Where greater specificity is important-particularly in relation to governance structures, institutional representation, and interpretation of the findings-the report uses more precise distinctions where possible. The lobbying registry data analyzed in this study include First Nations governments and tribal councils, Métis governments and settlements, Inuit governments and regional organizations, Indigenous economic development corporations, and Indigenous advocacy organizations.

title: Strategic Tax Architecture and Foreign Direct Investment Resilience in Resource-Rich Nigeria
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Birmingham City University, University of Dundee, University of Wolverhampton, Edinburgh Napier University and Northumbria University

detail.title: Strategic Tax Architecture and Foreign Direct Investment Resilience in Resource-Rich Nigeria
detail.abstract: Foreign direct investment is increasingly being contested on the basis of strategy, institutional credibility, and policy predictability rather than tax cuts alone. This paper examines how Nigeria's corporate tax architecture shapes foreign direct investment (FDI) resilience by distinguishing between company income tax, petroleum profit tax, and tertiary education tax, while controlling for exchange-rate conditions. Using annual Nigerian data reported for 1990-2018 and an error-correction modelling framework, the study shows a long-run relationship among FDI and the fiscal variables. Company income tax is positively associated with FDI in the long run, whereas the tertiary education tax is negative and statistically significant. Petroleum profit tax and exchange rate effects are directionally plausible but statistically weak. The error-correction term is negative and significant, indicating rapid adjustment after disequilibrium. The findings challenge a simple tax-minimisation view of multinational location choice and suggest that investors also read tax revenue as a signal of market scale, institutional capacity and public-goods commitment. The paper advances a strategic tax-architecture perspective for emerging economies seeking both revenue mobilisation and investment competitiveness.

title: Reducing the digital divide for marginalized households
affiliations: University of Bologna, University of Bologna, Department of Economics and University of Bologna

detail.title: Reducing the digital divide for marginalized households
detail.abstract: Digital skills are essential for social inclusion, labor market participation, and effective engagement with children in an increasingly digital environment, yet many adults in high-income countries lack even basic competencies. Despite growing public investment - reflected, for example, in European initiatives such as the Digital Decade and the substantial resources allocated under the Next Generation EU framework - causal evidence on how to effectively build digital skills among disadvantaged populations, who typically lie in the left tail of the skill distribution, remains limited. We design and implement a randomized controlled trial evaluating a comprehensive digital inclusion intervention that jointly addresses financial and learning barriers to technology adoption. The study involves 859 low-income families with school-aged children in Italy, randomly assigned to a control group or to one of two treatment arms providing a tablet, free internet access, and digital literacy training of different intensity. One year after the intervention, both treatment arms generate large and persistent gains in digital skills, with no systematic differences across arms, as well as substantial improvements in digital parenting practices and use of online public services. Mediation analysis shows that gains in digital skills, rather than access alone, drive these broader outcomes. Effects on labor market outcomes are limited to expectations, suggesting the presence of binding structural constraints. Overall, our findings demonstrate that relatively modest, scalable interventions can generate meaningful digital inclusion gains.

title: The Behavioral Consequences of Positive and Negative Affect: A Cross-Sectional Study of Burnout, Job Satisfaction, and Emotional Intelligence Among Healthcare Workers in Central Ethiopia
